note_sources.text: : Padrón 1964 Anniversary Series. The cigars were famously introduced at the peek of the great cigar boom, commemorating 30 years since José Orlando Padrón opened shop in Miami in 1964. The Padrón 1964 Anniversary Series was introduced in 1994 to commemorate our company’s 30th anniversary. This line consists of eleven sizes that are all available in sun-grown natural and maduro wrappers. All tobacco used in this limited production series is aged for four years, creating a smooth and complex flavor. In honor of the age-old Cuban tradition of box-pressing cigars, the 1964 Anniversary line was introduced as a box-pressed series. For the protection of our customers we have introduced measures to safeguard against counterfeiting with a specially designed double band, featuring an individually-numbered guarantee label. The Padrón 1964 Anniversary Series is consistently ranked by industry experts as one of the top brands in the world. Padrón Cigars Since this time, Padrón has debuted equally acclaimed smoking experiences (1926 Serie and Family Reserve), as well as many expansions to the 1964 series itself. The latest additions came in the summer of 2017 with the Soberano and Presidente —both representing the first tubo releases for the famed 1964 Anniversary Series. These releases followed in the footsteps of Padrón’s 1926 Serie No. 90 tubo cigars from the year prior, only the 1964 cigars retained their box-pressed shapes; boasting a pronounced and unorthodox box-shaped tubo presentation. SEE ALSO: Padrón 1926 Serie No. 90 Natural Review & Rating 1964 Anniversary Series Presidente Maduro Breakdown Wrapper: Nicaraguan Sun-Grown (4-year-aged) Binder: Nicaraguan Sun-Grown (4-year-aged) Filler: Nicaraguan Sun-Grown (4-year-aged) Factory: Tabacos Cubanica S.A. (Nicaragua) Production: Regular Production Vitola: 6″ × 50 “Presidente” (Toro) Price: $15.50 (MSRP) The Soberano (5″ x 52) and Presidente (6″ × 50) were the primary focus for Padrón at the 2017 IPCPR trade show. While the cigars are the same blend as the traditional 1964, they mark two new sizes for the brand. At the time of release, we wrote: Previously, the closest to these vitolas were the Belicoso (5″ x 52) and Torpedo (6″ x 52) vitolas, but these both showcased figurado-style heads. The unique aspect of this release is that both cigars are presented in square-shaped tubes, rather the traditional, round, aluminum containers used for tubo cigars. Nearly every Padrón cigar, with the exception of releases within the last two years, have been box-pressed and the Soberano & Presidente highlight this quite nicely. Appearance Obviously it is the metal containers that set this cigar apart visually. This is a very classy presentation, showing a golden top piece that slides off of a cream-colored bottom. The look closely resembles the beloved 1964 band, complete with an intricate pattern to match the counter-fit-proof sub-band (albeit without the numbering found on a standard 1964 band). These tubes are fairly thick and feel more substantial than an ordinary tubo cylinder. My only real gripe is the same as with the Padrón 1926 Serie No. 90 tubo: that the cigar’s are celloed and that there is no cedar lining on the inside of the tube. This is certainly not a deal breaker, but it seems like a missed opportunity to further set the cigars apart as an upgraded experience. Tube removed, the cigar looks identical to any former 1964 Maduro (i.e. no new sub-bands, etc.). There is the familiar box-pressed shape and dark, chocolatey hue. The wrapper leaf has a muted/matte sheen to it, with a velvety texture between the fingers. There are dark and easily visible veins, some random color variations, and well-placed wrapper seams. The toro feels slightly light in weight, with what looks to be a medium bunch. From head to toe, there are perhaps a few soft spots on one of my smoking samples. It’s a nice size, one you’d expect would’ve been a staple in this classic series since the get-go. The maduro shows classic notes of leather, animal musk, and medium-roast coffee on the wrapper. There are added aromas of mocha, loads of brownie batter, and a touch of terrarium on the cigar’s foot. With a straight cut, I found a medium/firm pre-light draw and notes of leather, cocoa, and a long-lasting menthol burn on the back of the throat. Click images below for full resolution Smoking Experience The first few puffs from the Presidente Maduro are not what I had expected. Where the cigar is often sweet and full of flavor, these flavors were of wild herb, raw peppercorn, and almost in “harsh” territory. Thankfully, this settles only moments later, replaced with white pepper spice in the retrohale, chocolate, coffee, and cream on the finish. But it is perhaps the raw tobacco against the tongue that is the standout experience up to this point—with the perfect amount of tartness to keep the tongue engaged. The draw is around medium-plus (7/10), which is close to perfect but maybe slightly too firm at times. This makes for a medium-plus smoke output—slightly above anticipated and very much welcomed. In the cigar’s early stages, there are signs of a stark white ash (flakey, with medium-gray layers) and a wavy burn line that appears to be burning right on schedule. The cigar’s profile is medium in strength, full in flavor, and medium-plus in body. With notes of mineral/rain, stone fruit, deep chocolate, coffee, and vanilla on the finish, flavor output is huge. The cigar seems to be firing on all cylinders as it transitions from the first to second third, with unmistakable flavors that even the ardent “anti-intangible-flavor” snob couldn’t deny. Behind the obvious notes mentioned, there are background components of corn chips and dark fig pudding that help round out the experience as the initial white pepper spice begins to dwindle. Padron 1964 Anniversary Maduro Series cigars take everything we know and love from the natural version and adds a spicy Nicaraguan maduro wrapper. The 1964 Anniversary line was introduced in the mid 90s to commemorate the brand's 30th year in business. Throughout its existence, the 1964 line has earned countless accolades and joins the rest of the ultra-premium Padron cigars as one of the most decorated cigars in history. All tobacco used in the 1964 Anniversary Maduro is sun-grown Nicaraguan habano grown on the world-famous Padron farms, aged at least 4 years before production.

note_sources.text: Padron Maduro is the dark, chocolatey version of the celebrated Padron Original Series cigar that has become known as one of the greatest cigars on the planet. The Padron legacy began in 1964 and has shown no sign of slowing down, as year after year the company produces some of the finest cigars money can buy, with something for everyone. Whether an ultra-premium celebration cigar or a consistent, well-made everyday smoke, Padron never misses the mark. Padron Maduro is rolled with 100% sun-grown Nicaraguan habano tobacco, which undergoes aging for a minimum of two and a half years. It is an icon in the world of fine maduro cigars.

note_sources.text: Padron Natural is the true connoisseur's go-to cigar. The Padron legacy dates back to the 60s when brand owner and patriarch Jose O. Padron fled Cuba and started a small Miami cigar factory from scratch. What began as an iffy, no-name business has since become one of the most dominant cigar companies on the planet. Padron Natural consists completely of top-shelf sun-grown Nicaraguan Habano tobacco—wrapper, filler, and binder. It's medium-full and incomparably consistent in construction, taste, and quality. Today, each and every Padron cigar is expertly produced in the legendary Padron factory in Nicaragua.

note_sources.text: Because of the strange construction on the head, I went the safe route and did a narrow V-cut instead of a guillotine cut (this puts less pressure on the cigar’s shape). The cold draw had flavors of white pepper, earthy cocoa, and white chocolate. After lighting, the smoking draw was agreeable and did not give me issues in the early portions of the smoking experience. The first puffs introduced red pepper, anise, and additional cocoa (but a little deeper, like a 90 percent chocolate bar). The ash was white from the get-go and it had very little smoke—not an optimal start. After about 10 minutes, the robusto started canoeing and became quite uneven. After my first touchup, the flavors started to change drastically into what I will term “gamey.” Have you ever had a bison burger or grilled lamb that was somewhat charred? This was very similar. The retrohale was sharp, showing zesty sensations of burnt peppercorn. The strength was medium with a long finish. At the end of the first third, coffee notes appeared with a sweet molasses aftertaste. Throughout this section, the aroma of the cigar was very interesting—a charred biscuit, similar to starting a BBQ except it was not smoky—definitely campfire smells but more subdued… falling short of the fire department running in to extinguish it. Click images below for full resolution In the second third, flavors in the retrohale morphed into peanuts—salty, creamy peanuts that had me wanting to make a PB&J sandwich and down it with some fresh-squeezed milk. I’m lactose intolerant, but I didn’t care at that moment… The rest of the second third can be described as a combo of cream, sweet sun-drenched red pepper, molasses, sourdough bread, and a touch of cinnamon, with peanuts at the forefront. The second third is the sweet spot and this cigar’s superpower—I wish we could have stayed here, for the rating would have been higher. The final third begins and the burn/ash begin to even out—I’m very excited for other tastes to evolve. But DAMN, I spoke too soon and the inevitable begins to unfold. It’s the same profile from before, but now the flavors become very bitter and charcoal removes the dream that was the second third. Strength-wise, the robusto is at a high medium but never goes the full nicotine pounce. The only new flavor that’s introduced is roasted vegetables, with the ash turning a tarry brown. The last third is not enjoyable at all and flavors become very acidic; I found myself spitting more than a sailor at a baseball game with his Kodiak snuff. This is where I stopped and finished the smoking experience because of all the chaotic burn issues. I didn’t get even close to nubbing it, since the last third was only smoked for about an inch before putting it out.
note_sources.title: Partagas 1845 Clásico Robusto

note_sources.text: The Partagas 1845 cigar, as though the brand's original offerings hadn't long ago vanquished any pretenders to the crown, seeks to emphasize the iconic Partagas name as #1 among full-bodied fanatics. To build upon the world-class reputation their cigars are known, for, only a man with his own world-class reputation would suffice, and lucky for us, the renowned Benji Menendez was up to the task. To accomplish his mission, Benji created an exclusive blend of only the most select ligero and seco from the best Dominican and Nicaraguan tobaccos that had already been taken to the next level by being aged in Dominican rum barrels. To this exquisite mix he added a proprietary Connecticut Habano binder before finishing with an Ecuadorian Habano Viso wrapper. From the very first puffs through the smooth draw, the flavors are naturally creamy and leathery, solidly medium-bodied and enticing. Paired with a malty Highland Scotch, this cigar makes for an awesome after-dinner treat, although it can be enjoyed just about any time. Unless you're just picking up a single to try, both journeyman and expert smokers alike will find themselves burning through their stash at a pretty good clip, so we recommend stocking up, or restocking, now. You'll find the Partagas 1845 an excellent humidor companion to smokes such as the Camacho Select and Padilla Reserva Habano.

note_sources.text: Heritage begins with classic flavors (as it should) of barnyard hay, rich leather, and a subtle, floral sweetness. The body is on the mild side, though the actual flavor output is more towards medium. On the construction side, the cigar shows a slightly tight draw, producing medium clouds of smoke on each puff (more smoke than expected from the draw). The burn is wavy, carrying the ash to about half an inch before requiring a quick touchup. note_sources.title: Partagas Heritage Robusto

note_sources.text: If you're going to name a cigar the Partagas Heritage, you had better make sure it lives up to the hype. Fortunately, this smoke comes from a company that has been making wickedly delicious stogies for what seems like forever, and the Heritage is more than able to hold its own against any other premium cigar past or present. Beneath the expertly fermented Honduran Olancho San Agustin wrapper lies a Connecticut Broadleaf binder perfectly matched to the complex filler blend of Dominican Piloto Cubano, Mexican San Andres, and Honduran Jamastran longleaf to create a classic and full flavor you'll want to savor. From the very moment you pull the first one from the box, the Partagas Heritage begins delivering a smoking experience steeped in tradition. With a red and gold band that celebrates the best the brand has to offer, each generously rolled vitola is a ruddy brown marvel of craftsmanship that smells of leather and fertile earth. Upon lighting, a warm rush of cedar and dark chocolate greets the palate, followed soon by buttered wheat toast topped with a touch of honey. Bright spice smoothed by a rich caramel creaminess enters before reaching the midpoint, the smoke staying cool and lush even as the strength reaches a steady medium-plus. The long-burning final third is punctuated by Irish coffee, almonds, and hints of toasted marshmallow. Perfect for both longtime fans of time-honored tastes and those aficionados seeking to expand their horizons, make history come alive today by filling your humidor with a selection of fine Partagas Heritage cigars. They'll be the perfect companions to the Camacho Coyolar and Punch Gran Puros you no doubt already have in your cart.

note_sources.text: The first puff tastes like toasted marshmallow and campfire—it reminds me of s’mores with a toasty sweetness. The draw is slightly tight to begin, taking a bit of extra effort to get some smoke rolling. As it progresses, the Partagas Legend brings notes of sweet oak and whisky; combined with some of the toasted flavor from before, there is almost a bourbon-barrel flavor to it. At close to the one-inch mark, the burn gets slightly wonky on me and I have to touch up. While the flavor output is medium, strength and body are both hovering around medium-plus. Partagas Legend may look like a natural, but the cigar smokes like a maduro, at least in its early portions. As herbal notes begin to appear, I’m impressed by some of the quick flavor changes within the cigar’s beginning.
note_sources.title: Partagas Legend Corona Extra Leyenda

note_sources.text: The Partagas Legend cigar exemplifies the fact that success is never a singular affair, often taking a team of exceptionally talented people years to achieve. This premium smoke honors five men, five legends, who all played a crucial role in making Partagas the acclaimed brand it is to this day. Even the longleaf tobacco types comprising each shimmering vitola, from the Connecticut Broadleaf wrapper, to the San Agustin Olancho binder from Honduras, as well as the Dominican Piloto Cubano filler, were specifically selected as much for their historical significance as for their exceptionally rich taste. In other words, this might be their crowning achievement. Appearing at first like ebony thanks to the contrasting bright white and beautifully embossed band hugging the firmly packed barrel, the expertly fermented wrapper is actually closer to a robust cocoa hue. A complimentary chocolatey aroma heightens the impression, while the oily sheen urges the knuckle to grip just a bit tighter lest the Partagas Legend slip away. Pulling a good flame into the cigar, you can expect the palate to first discover a rush of espresso, cedar, and leather. With the profile hitting its full-bodied stride early, hints of black cherry, molasses, graham cracker, and marzipan are just as prompt to sweeten the potently earthy and spice-laden base flavors for the long journey ahead. Perhaps you've overlooked or even forgotten about Partagas, thinking them a relic of an earlier age when cigars were not nearly as exciting as some of today's stogies. Let the Partagas Legend show you what you've been missing while your off enjoying other excellent smokes crafted to celebrate many years in the business, like the Perdomo Twentieth Anniversary Maduro or the Nat Cicco 1965 Aniversario.

The profile holds largely similar within the first two-plus inches, having a solid flavor foundation and impressing in the construction department as well. This includes a straight medium-gray ash (holding for at least two inches) and an unwavering burn line. note_sources.title: Perdomo Reserve 10th Anniversary Box-Pressed Maduro Epicure

note_sources.text: Celebrating a decade since the debut of the world-renowned Perdomo Reserve Champagne line, the Perdomo Reserve 10th Anniversary Maduro is a masterful cigar built for special occasions and seasoned aficionados alike. Crafted in Nicaragua under the guidance of Nick Perdomo, this Maduro is the sister cigar to the Perdomo Reserve 10th Anniversary Sun Grown, forming a Nicaraguan puro with a wrapper, filler, and binder aged no less than six years. What sets the Maduro apart is its rich Nicaraguan Maduro wrapper, carefully aged for 14 additional months in bourbon barrels—a hallmark of the Reserve Champagne series. Rated 91 by Cigar Aficionado and 93 by Cigar Journal , the Perdomo Reserve 10th Anniversary Maduro was also honored as Cigar of the Year by Cigar Journal, cementing its status as a top-tier Nicaraguan cigar. This blend delivers a luxurious smoking experience that impresses even the most discerning aficionados. Both the Maduro and Sun Grown editions are the long-awaited sequels to the original Perdomo Reserve 10th Anniversary Champagne, which featured a Connecticut wrapper. The Maduro completes the “Perdomo Trifecta,” offering aficionados a unique wrapper variation alongside the classic and Sun Grown editions. Expertly rolled and box-pressed, the Perdomo Reserve 10th Anniversary Maduro wears a sophisticated blue and gold band with the iconic Perdomo Reserve logo. Every vitola delivers an effortless draw and generous, thick smoke. On the palate, the Maduro opens with bold Nicaraguan pepper, a signature spice that lingers throughout the smoke. Earthy notes of raw tobacco and dark chocolate dominate the flavor profile, complemented by hints of coffee, brown sugar, and oak . A subtle sweetness on the finish—thanks to the bourbon barrel aging—adds a memorable, refined touch. Medium-full-bodied, this blend is rich, smooth, and supremely satisfying. Perfect for cigar connoisseurs and seasoned smokers, the Perdomo Reserve 10th Anniversary Maduro impresses with complexity and craftsmanship. Ideal for marking special celebrations, unwinding after a long week, or pairing with coffee, bourbon, or port wine, this cigar is best enjoyed on a full stomach due to its robust body. Comparable in stature yet more refined than the Perdomo Reserve Champagne Noir, the Maduro demonstrates the masterful blending skills of Perdomo’s expert team. Though released slightly after the true 10th anniversary, this limited-edition cigar is a rare gem destined to be remembered as one of Perdomo’s finest Nicaraguan cigars. Experience the Perdomo Reserve 10th Anniversary Maduro, a luxurious, limited-edition Nicaraguan cigar perfect for collectors and aficionados seeking a sophisticated, flavorful smoke.

note_sources.text: Perla del Mar Corojo hits just as you’d expect from a Corojo wrapper. That sweetness on the lips and tongue is bright and vibrant, with a fruity citrus aroma that adds a refreshing compliment. The retrohale brings it home, with the Nicaraguan filler tobaccos offering a white pepper spice that is mild to medium in intensity.

note_sources.text: Ventura Cigar Co. is coming on like gangbusters. Not only with their unique packaging for their cigars, but also with the different blends that are inside. Psyko Seven Maduro is just another example of the great cigars that this new cigar maker is putting out. Mild-to-medium in body, Psyko Seven Maduro comes wrapped in a prescription to sit back and relax. Made with the same unique 5-country blend as the natural, the maduro version is wrapped in a dark San Andres wrapper. (See more PSyKo Seven cigars ) Psyko Seven Maduro may start out with a huge pepper blast on your palate; this quickly subsides into an amazingly smooth mild cigar. The San Andres wrapper provides a subtle sweetness to the lips as well as each puff. As you delve deeper into this cigar, you will find rich notes of cedar, spice, and cocoa. Sit back and relax with a Psyko Seven Maduro. This is just the cigar that the doctor ordered to start out the day with a nice cup of dark roast coffee. For a more mild experience, we would recommend the lighter colored wrapper version of this same cigar.

SEE ALSO: General Cigar Debuts Punch Diablo When it came time to select the blend for Diablo, we decided that we wanted to make the fullest-bodied Punch to date. AJ Fernandez is a master when it comes to developing full-bodied cigars, so we asked him to create a blend using aged tobaccos, one that has strength and bold flavor to complement the rest of the cigars under the Punch umbrella. We’re confident that the blend he delivered will be a great new option for classic Punch smokers and that Diablo will give all full-bodied smokers another reason to experience Punch. Ed Lahmann, senior brand manager for Punch Click images below for full resolution Punch Diablo Scamp Breakdown Wrapper: Ecuadorian Sumatra Oscuro Binder: Connecticut Broadleaf Filler: Nicaraguan Habano | Honduran Habano Factory: Tabacalera A.J. Fernandez Cigars de Nicaragua (Nicaragua) Production: Regular Vitola: 6⅛” x 50 “Scamp” (Toro) Price: $7.19 (SRP) With A.J. handling the blend, it’s no surprise that Diablo comes loaded with Nicaraguan and Connecticut Broadleaf tobaccos. But it’s the age of the leaves used that wasn’t quite as expected, with the Ecuadorian Sumatra Oscuro wrapper carrying four years at the time the blend was rolled, a six-year-aged binder, and four-year-aged fillers. Punch Diablo debuted in three sizes: Scamp (6⅛” x 50), Diabolus (5¼” x 54), and Brute (6¼” x 60), with the former two available in boxes of 25, while the Brute is sold in boxes of 20 cigars. The cigars were released in July, with prices ranging from $7 to $8. Appearance The Punch Diablo is sporting a new, bolder look for the Punch brand, with a black band and red accents that really bring out the meaty color and texture of the oscuro wrapper. The Diablo box packaging has “The Dark Side of Punch” emblazoned on the inner lid, which, looking at the dark and leathery exterior of the cigar, makes perfect sense. The wrapper has the appearance of one solid chunk of tobacco, with no real visible veins. The aroma coming from the cigar is of deep rich cedar and maybe a little ammonia—it reminds me of stepping foot into an aging room at a factory. Click images below for full resolution Smoking Experience This cigar starts strong, like really strong. I feel like this cigar went off to war when it was 18 and never really talks about it much… I get nice notes of wood and a nutty flavor that is a bit overshadowed by the strength of the cigar. About an inch in, the strength calms down a bit and smooth, meaty nuances begin to appear. This cigar is interesting because it seems to vary a great deal in terms of body and strength, but has been a bit one-noted in complexity thus far. Diablo would pair well with some sparkling water or a martini, allowing the heavy tobaccos to take center stage. Just before the halfway point the Diablo starts to loosen up a little bit, showing added notes of citrus and hay. Soon enough, dark flavors join the mix, all of which (not so) coincidentally begin with the word “black.” Black cherry, black pepper, black licorice… it’s all there. In terms of texture, it’s a bit of a dry smoke, but that is not necessarily a bad thing, only requiring extra sips of some sparkling water. Just before the band the Punch Diablo starts to hit its stride, with smoke oozing from every puff. It has the nice complexity of the black-themed middle of the cigar, with the strength from the beginning. The Diablo is really strong, and I’m not one of those guys that says, “You should eat before you smoke this cigar,” but you really should eat before you smoke this cigar! As a person who doesn’t gravitate towards cigars that really “punch” you in the face (excuse that horrible pun), I’d asses this is a nice version of strength. Moving past the band, I have to compliment the construction of the cigar; I have only had to relight once (and that might have been user error) and the burn has been razor sharp the whole time. The latest stretch has been almost flavorless and I can tell my dance with the devil has come to an end.

note_sources.text: Punch Diablo marks the first time that a Punch cigar will be made outside of Honduras, where the brand has been made since the 1960s. Ed Lahmann, senior brand manager for Punch said, “When it came time to select the blend for Diablo, we decided that we wanted to make the fullest-bodied Punch to date. AJ Fernandez is a master when it comes to developing full-bodied cigars, so we asked him to create a blend using aged tobaccos, one that has strength and bold flavor to complement the rest of the cigars under the Punch umbrella. We’re confident that the blend he delivered will be a great new option for classic Punch smokers and that Diablo will give all full-bodied smokers another reason to experience Punch.” The devil is in the details, so Master Blender AJ Fernandez has left nothing to chance with this four-country blend. Punch Diablo is made with a blend of four-year-aged Nicaraguan and Honduran Habano leaves and is wrapped in an oscuro Ecuadoran Sumatra wrapper, also aged four years. The Connecticut Broadleaf binder has been aged for six years. Handcrafted at Tabacalera AJ Fernandez, Punch Diablo will make its debut in packaging that features the brand’s new design. These three sizes will be available, beginning in late July: Scamp (6.125 x 50); SRP per cigar $7.19; 25 cigars per box Diabolus (5.25 x 54); SRP per cigar $7.79; 25 cigars per box Brute (6.25 x 60); SRP per cigar $8.19; 20 cigars per box By loading the video, you agree to YouTube’s privacy policy. Learn more Load video Always unblock YouTube

Punch cigars have always had a reputation for diabolical deliciousness and strength, but the new Punch Diablo will take your poor innocent palate to depths of flavor and complexity you never knew existed. Who else could have wrought this devilish delight but the current reigning master of tobacco, A.J. Fernandez. Tasked with developing a potent blend that would leave in smoldering ruin all other pretenders to the throne on which Punch sits, A.J. first summoned a host of 4-year-aged Nicaraguan and Honduran Habano ligero to serve as filler. He then formed an alliance between a hefty Connecticut Broadleaf binder and a spicy Ecuadoran Sumatra Oscuro wrapper, aged 6 and 4 years respectively, and gave them preeminence over the filler to create a cigar of awesome character.

Halfway through and I am still getting a lot of cedar flavors with spice, but now the finish has warmed up and I taste a bit of caramel or molasses . This is a full flavor , full bodied cigar, so make sure you are smoking it on a full stomach because this baby is a powerhouse . Past the 2/3rds mark and no further flavor changes, but I am really enjoying the finish on this cigar – warm, sweet spice with cedar overtones . Would I smoke this cigar again? Indeed! note_sources.text: Manuel Quesada is known for not only making some unbelievable cigars but also experimenting with strains of tobacco leaf which are very rare. Quesada Jalapa fits both of these categories. Made in the Dominican Republic, this vitola is filled with premium aged Dominican and Nicaraguan filler and has a Dominican binder. The experimental part of this cigar is the wrapper. Grown by the Plascencia family in Nicaragua, the Nicaraguan Jalapa wrapper is what gives this cigar not only its name but the bulk of its flavor. Only a few hundred bales of this rare tobacco were produced, and only 1000 boxes of each size of the Quesada Jalapa were made. (See more Quesada Cigars ) A gorgeous black, white and gold band adorns this wrapper and almost matches how majestic the wrapper looks. Light brown in hue, it would take a microscope to find a flaw. Just as wonderful as the wrapper leaf looks is how it burns. Perfect and straight, this cigar holds onto its ash until you feel obligated to tip it off. Once lit, there is a creaminess to the smoke that is matched with a note of cedar and pepper. The main thing to note is an unbelievable smoothness from beginning to end. The second half of the Quesada Jalapa brings in flavors of leather and coffee which marry amazingly with the spiciness from before. Quesada Jalapa is yet another unique cigar from the mind of Manuel Quesada. This is an amazing chance to smoke an extremely rare wrapper, but due to its uniqueness this is a very limited production cigar. The flavors matched amazingly with a port after dinner. Another wonderful Quesada cigar is the Oktoberfest.

From first light, it’s quickly evident that MQ 70 is a complex creature, showcasing delicate nuances of toasted wood, nut shells, and leather. The smoke can be completely exhaled through the nostrils—differing from the spicy blast through the retrohale at most cigar’s beginnings. The smoke output is on the lighter side of medium; however, it offers a sticky, pasty texture that makes for a longer finish and a stick-to-your-ribs experience that really lets you know it’s there! A near-perfect burn performs a sudden one-eighty, requiring decent touchups at the half-inch and one-inch marks. This is the only true criticism thus far—with poor smoke output and canoeing burn lines coming in sudden and sporadic bursts. On the flavor side, MQ 70 is magnificent, showcasing endless complexities. It is somewhat difficult to sum it all up, as the flavors seem to hit every angle of the palate; much in the same way you’ll find with many Cubans. The cigar manages to offer a contrasting experience, with dark and robust notes (toasted nuts and leather), delivered through a delicate, light, and clean
note_sources.title: Manuel Quesada 70th

note_sources.text: A cigar blended by Manuel Quesada, in his taste profile, to celebrate his 70th birthday and to be Manuel Quesada go to Cigars. Made in his two favorite sizes, a belicoso and a toro, come and celebrate with him and discover the tastes, aromas and sensations that Manuel Quesada enjoys. (See more Quesada Cigars ) Cigar aficionados will testify to the fact that a Manuel Quesada 70th cigar is one that should be taken seriously in the cigar universe. These cigars are known for their heady blends which make the taste of each cigar unique. The master blender from Manuel Quesada Cigars, Manuel Quesada himself, has created a fine cigar, the Manuel Quesada 70th. When Manuel Quesada created the Manuel Quesada 70th, he wanted it to be a stand-alone cigar, but also a cigar that people would instantly go to for a cigar taste anytime. While this is a limited-edition cigar among cigars, it is an honestly rare one. It has instant viewing appeal with a Dominican wrapper and a binder from Sumatra. You can easily tell that this is a cigar from Manuel Quesada as it comes in two famous sizes, a toro and a belicoso. If you are tasting a cigar for the first time, you can try this one as it doesn't hit you quite so hard as many cigars might. The Manuel Quesada 70th has all the richness in taste that the master blender himself loves, but it is a cigar for the people. The filler is hand-selected with accents of Nicaragua and the Dominican Republic. Some experts argue that the cigar has complicated notes with fruity blends and earthy tones. The nuts are also present, but every ingredient has a good balance. The family of Quesada has been in the cigar creation business for more than a century. The history of cigar making and this family dates back to bakers arriving from Spain, into Cuba. In the latter part of the 1800s, the family broke into the cigar business with a bang. They are even known to having paid debts in the form of tobacco. In later years, the family made the Dominican Republic its home, Manuel Quesada prospered and made Quesada cigars household name among cigar smokers. Manuel Quesada has managed, with his two daughters to make a variety of blends to suit every cigar fan. You cannot mistake the taste of any cigar from this reliable cigar company, whether it's the Quesada 1974 Lancero or the Manuel Quesada 70th.

After toasting and lighting the cigar with a soft double-flame lighter, the first few draws deliver notes of hay and mustiness, which is usually characteristic of aged Dominican tobacco. These initial flavors are quickly enhanced with touches of cedar, coffee, dried earth, and natural tobacco. The draw of the robusto is very open—perhaps too open—generating an above-average amount of smoke output. Additional aromas and flavors of assorted nuts, cocoa powder, and dried fruits mingle with the primary notes, while must and red pepper are dominant on the retrohale. As the Barber Pole enters into its second third it begins to display the following general characteristics—medium in body, medium in strength, and medium in flavor. The aromas and flavors present in the first third of the cigar continue to dominate the profile, while a cherry and carbonated soda note appears at intervals, like the Cheerwine soda I drank as a kid when visiting relatives in North Carolina. The smoke is rather dry, requiring frequent sips of San Pellegrino—my preferred beverage when reviewing cigars. Room aroma is a rather delicate combination of old paper and natural tobacco, reminiscent of sitting next to a cigar smoker wearing a woolen overcoat which has never been dry cleaned in a small reading room at a used book store. The burn line wavers a bit, holding an inch and a half of flakey nickel ash, highlighted with streaks of onyx between the stacks. On the retrohale, the must and red pepper present in the first third is enhanced with a quality which can only be described as fizzy. As it burns through its final third, the Barber Pole begins a slow stall. The draw becomes extremely open, requiring delicate and controlled puffs to prevent the cigar from overheating. A strong amount of bitterness and saltiness develops as the robusto inches its way toward the nub, prompting a search in the refrigerator for a sweeter beverage pairing. After a few more draws, the cigar is placed in an ashtray and allowed to incinerate.
note_sources.title: Quesada Reserva Privada Barber Pole Robusto

note_sources.text: Quesada Reserva Privada Cigars is rated 92 in Cigar Aficionado. The Dominican crop of 1997 was extraordinary, and Manuel "Manolo" Quesada saved a large number of pounds of tobacco from this crop. Blending the fillers of 1997 with Dominican tobaccos we are currently using, with a splash of Pennsylvania fillers. These cigars are brimming with a tapestry of scrumptious flavors including earth, cocoa, pepper, sweet spice, and wood. (See more Quesada Cigars ) The Quesada Reserva Privada cigar is another beauty from a family famous for creating some of the world's finest blends. Manuel and his team of highly skilled rollers fashion these fine sticks using a Dominican Criollo binder, along with vintage Dominican and US Pennsylvania ligero tobacco for the filler.

The Oscuro takes a bit longer than average to toast—probably due to the heavy wrapper. The first impressions are of a very smooth smoke, not particularly spicy, as you might expect. Through a medium resistance draw, the cigar produces slightly under average smoke output. There’s a hint of spice in the retrohale, but mostly notes of chocolate-covered cherries, stone fruit, and a dry, black pepper on the finish. The profile is much softer than expected, with a silky mouthfeel and no obvious/dominating flavor aspects. The feel of the cigar is great, giving an oily residue on the lips and a salty zest from the raw tobacco against the tongue. Moving forward, there’s a clean and fizzy sensation in the retrohale and on the tongue, it’s refreshing but bites, like carbonated soda. I wouldn’t say this lasts long though, only around the first-third. In the middle of the stick, the flavors take a bit of a dive. The experience is quite dry, having notes of oak, dry cocoa, burning brush, and occasionally harsh aspects. I’d peg it around medium body, with medium flavors and medium-plus strength. The ash is quite flakey and falls fairly regularly—around every half inch to one inch. This is possibly due to the frequent touchups needed, which in turn seem to be due to the cigar’s heavy wrapper. The brighter sides of this section show tasty notes of dark porter and roasted malts. For a portion of the final third, flavors continue in this vein—dark, leathery, very dry, burnt bread, increasing strength, etc. But the Oscuro takes a surprising turn at around the mid-point of this third. Black licorice, a pinching spice in the retro, and sweet cedar suddenly appear. This is soon joined by an added complexity of cinnamon and clove, giving just the right balance of sweetness, complexity, and strength for a very fun finale.
note_sources.title: Quesada Reserva Privada Oscuro

note_sources.text: Now to the cigar itself. The broadleaf wrapper has a very nice, musty, chocolate aroma. The cold draw shows a decent performance, foreshadowing a sweet pepper and just a hint of earthy notes. Lighting up the cigar, a slightly loose draw brings out a huge blast of pepper and spice right off the first light. A deep, slightly sweet spice and cocoa infusion really weighs heavy on my palate. The retro-hale adds a bit more of a spice bite, and also a general sweet tobacco. Getting past the first light, the cigar simmers down to medium body. As I make my way into the first third, not a whole lot has changed thus far. A full-flavored white pepper and spice control the flavors. The finish is very long at this point and quite spicy (not my cup o’ tea). The retro-hale also mellowed out, adding more sweetness than anything else, but not quite enough to be very noticeable. The burn has been going fairly well thus far, and the ash seems to be holding on for a good inch or so. Reaching about the halfway mark, I start to experience some issues. I seem to be drawing lots of air—but no smoke. What’s this? Tunneling. It’s always a sad day when tunneling starts in a cigar (filler/binder burning more quickly than wrapper), and I rapidly began to try and fix the situation. After I burn a good quarter inch of wrapper down, I start to smoke the Prohibition again. It seems to be smoking decent now, and I continue on my way. Beverage Pairing The Natural Brew Crème Soda—a bourbon vanilla soda, made from “the finest Madagascan Bourbon Vanilla Beans.” With my maduro, I decided to pair it with a lighter, sweeter drink than the average pairing. At this point in my cigar, pepper and spice have been the vocal majority in flavor, and a sweet, creamy drink sounds perfect to help liven it up. As I take the first sip, an overwhelmingly creamy and sweet vanilla relentlessly attacks my mouth. I have never tasted something so sweet and creamy. Pairing with the cigar, however, had lesser results than I had hoped. I expected the crème soda to bring out that natural sweetness I had first detected in the Prohibition, but instead it denounced any other flavors, and simply overwhelmed my palate with crème and sweet bourbon vanilla. With my cigar burning hot again, I begin down the end of the road. At this point, the cigar is still letting off rough notes of pepper and spice, and a general smooth sweetness—maybe a hint of baker’s chocolate. The draw has also changed, actually getting tighter; something rather unusual towards the end of a cigar—probably due to the tunneling problems. With that said, the cigar has remained very consistent with few transitions, but holds a well-balanced body profile, never going beyond a medium.
note_sources.title: Rocky Patel Prohibition – Broadleaf Maduro

note_sources.text: The new Rocky Patel Broadleaf cigar is a twist on a classic that just might redefine your expectations. There was a time not long after the fabled cigar boom when Connecticut wrappers were relegated to the mildest of stogies, with gentle flavors suitable mostly for grandmas and milquetoasts. Then came a surge of blending geniuses that proved shade-leaf could be used to enhance the flavor of more robust tobaccos, and while the original Rocky Patel Connecticut might not have been the first it was one of the more affordable of the tan and delicious premium cigars of that heady era. It is only natural then that an ebony-colored Connecticut Broadleaf is now paired with the original blend to add even more strength and complexity.

note_sources.text: e this cigar. A huge amount of flavorful smoke fills my my mouth and right off the bat I get a blast of coffee and chocolate . The finish taste on the smoke is a warm, salty carmel , which is extremely pleasant. As we work our way past the first third of this Rocky Patel, it’s rather clear this is a well made cigar, as the burn is perfect and the ash is firm and white . This is a medium to full bodied cigar but the flavors are full and satisfying. Halfway in and I am getting a really nice subtle spice along with a warm chocolate chip cookie flavor, the finish remains a constant melted caramel . I am really blown away by the construction on this cigar, which hints to the strict quality control at the Rocky Patel factory. Not once did I need to touch up or mess with the burn on this cigar, as it was perfect all the way to the end. These cigars will run about $7 per stick, which doesn’t exactly make them inexpensive in my book. Yet in the final analysis, I can’t say they are a bad value because they performed so well and the flavors were so pleasant. Would I smoke this cigar again? Yes, in fact this might be one of the best Rocky Patel cigars that I have smoked. I really enjoyed the warm carmel finish on each draw and I appreciate Rocky Patel’s desire to help fight for the rights of cigar smokers in the USA. If there's one thing an aficionado can count on in this crazy world, it's the fact that Rocky knows how to make flavorful stogies that won't bust your budget. Not to mention that his pursuit of the finest tobaccos over many years has resulted in a collection of frontmarks nearly unequaled in size or scope, meaning there's something for everyone. The Freedom Connecticut, a premium stick hand-built of aged Nicaraguan longleaf beneath a sleek and golden shade wrapper, will appeal to all smokers looking for a mild to medium delight that won't disappoint.

After I burn a good quarter inch of wrapper down, I start to smoke the Prohibition again. It seems to be smoking decent now, and I continue on my way. Beverage Pairing The Natural Brew Crème Soda—a bourbon vanilla soda, made from “the finest Madagascan Bourbon Vanilla Beans.” With my maduro, I decided to pair it with a lighter, sweeter drink than the average pairing. At this point in my cigar, pepper and spice have been the vocal majority in flavor, and a sweet, creamy drink sounds perfect to help liven it up. As I take the first sip, an overwhelmingly creamy and sweet vanilla relentlessly attacks my mouth. I have never tasted something so sweet and creamy. Pairing with the cigar, however, had lesser results than I had hoped. I expected the crème soda to bring out that natural sweetness I had first detected in the Prohibition, but instead it denounced any other flavors, and simply overwhelmed my palate with crème and sweet bourbon vanilla. With my cigar burning hot again, I begin down the end of the road. At this point, the cigar is still letting off rough notes of pepper and spice, and a general smooth sweetness—maybe a hint of baker’s chocolate. The draw has also changed, actually getting tighter; something rather unusual towards the end of a cigar—probably due to the tunneling problems. With that said, the cigar has remained very consistent with few transitions, but holds a well-balanced body profile, never going beyond a medium.
note_sources.title: Rocky Patel Prohibition – Broadleaf Maduro

note_sources.text: Rocky Patel has long been a staunch defender of cigar smoker's rights, and his new Prohibition line of premium cigars is a message to the FDA who is trying to impose on them. Packaged beautifully in branded mason jars, just like those used for moonshine during the prohibition on alcohol in the 1920s, this cigar is an amazingly well crafted 6 1/2" x 52 toro. Available in both a Connecticut broadleaf maduro wrapper as well as a San Andres Mexican leaf, these are made with filler and binder from Rocky's farm in Nicaragua. (See all Rocky Patel Cigars ) No matter which wrapper you choose, you will be great with a great tasting cigar. The filler blend gives flavors of spice and cedar and the notes of the wrapper change the complexity. The Connecticut broadleaf has a slightly sweeter mouthfeel that is layered with notes of coffee and leather. The San Andres wrapped stick has a slightly fuller body and features flavors of nuts and cedar as well as a long finish of dark cocoa. With the FDA trying to clamp down on premium cigars, leave it to Rocky Patel to make a statement with his cigars. Prohibition is not just that though, it is truly a great cigar as well. This flavors in both these cigars pairs perfectly with coffee and are smooth enough to enjoy any time of day.

specs.factory: TAVICUSA (Estelí, Nicaragua) Production: Regular release

note_sources.text: The immediate impression that hits my palate is one of a sweet and spicy nature. The spice is peppery and the sweetness that lingers on the palate and on the retrohale is one of honey. There are faint notes of licorice, graham cracker, and cashew in the first portion of the cigar. The smoke is cooler than most Connecticut Shade cigars. I find that many Shade-wrapped cigars tend to burn warmer by comparison, in my experience. The draw and construction through the first half of the cigar is solid, but I do grab my lighter a couple of times to touch up. Plenty of smoke is brought in with each puff, enveloping the palate with a long-lasting finish of cashew, pepper, nutmeg, and the dominant honey notes. As the smoke progresses, a quirky and unusual beef note comes into play and surprisingly melds well with the other flavors. It quickly dissipates, but it, nonetheless, is quite interesting and captivates my attention. While the flavor is plentiful, the body of this cigar remains low, creeping up only slightly and predictably nearing the final third. The deeper I get into the cigar, there is a building cream flavor that comes in forcefully, complimenting the pepper and honey quite well. As the cigar wraps up, the entire experience intensifies. The forceful cream note that came on like a whirlwind begins to dominate the palate, but the honey note starts to get a bit cloying. However, the pepper and oak notes on the retrohale quickly recuperate the flavor on the finish of this cigar. After the couple of touch-ups, the burn of the cigar holds steady and the draw remains consistent and solid throughout.
note_sources.title: Room101 Farce Connecticut Robusto

note_sources.text: After a very short-lived retirement from the tobacco business, jewelry tycoon and cigar aficionado Matt Booth made his daring return to the world of premium cigars, and after a couple amazing collaborations with Caldwell cigars, the first “new” cigar bearing the true Room 101 trademark was born: Room 101 Farce. Made at Tabacalera William Ventura in the Dominican Republic, Farce took the cigar world by storm at its debut, giving fans of the original Room 101 brand something to get excited about. The blend is comprised of an Ecuadorian wrapper leaf, a binder from Indonesia, and a delicious filler blend containing premium leaves from Nicaragua, Pennsylvania, and the Dominican Republic. What did the people think of this formidable comeback attempt? Well, we can let the remarkable 94 rating in Cigar Aficionado speak for itself, not to mention a spot on the Top 25 Cigars of 2019. As for packaging, Farce brings a whole new look to Room 101. The dark, refined bands and boxes give off a more serious feel than the old school Room 101s. However, the DNA is kept with the trademark Sakura flower boldly embossed in the center of the band. Construction-wise, things couldn’t be better. A solid pack and firm roll on the outside and an easy, overly productive draw on the inside make for a truly enjoyable smoking experience. The thick smoke greets the palate upon lighting with a burst of cedar and black pepper. Soon after, the rarely-used but rich and powerful Pennsylvania fillers make their impression felt, with bold, chocolaty flavor and a serious dose of vitamin N. Woody flavors meet hints of cinnamon and cocoa as the cigar progresses, and the finish is spicy and heavy. Though most of the way down this is a medium-full-bodied cigar, the strength really creeps up during the second half, turning Farce into an all-out full-bodied cigar. Though not exactly a cigar for newbies, Farce makes a great choice for someone looking to step up into the realm of fuller-bodied sticks. It goes without saying that those who will appreciate Farce the most are the ones fortunate enough to have enjoyed Matt Booth’s earlier concoctions. In that case, it is doubtless a must-try, for that classic feel that Room 101 has always been known for is definitely present here. Whether you’re a bourbon lover or someone who likes to sip on dark beer, Farce will pair beautifully. Though rich and strong it is never overpowering or harsh and tends to go with just about any fuller-bodied drink accompaniment. Cigars of similar stature may include Ashton VSG or Roma Craft CroMagnon . Matt Booth is back in business, and he’s back with a bang. See what the fuss is all about with Room 101 Farce.

specs.factory: Tabacalera William Ventura (Dominican Republic) Production: Regular Production

note_sources.text: The Ichiban has a nice tobacco aroma with just hints of coffee. On the cold draw, I could detect light pepper and wood, maybe oak, and some herbal notes as well. While toasting, a deep pepper and earth aroma floats heavily through the air in a nice, white, thick smoke. Huge amounts of chewy smoke rush in off the first draw, met with a full-bodied kick of pepper and earth that was just a little too harsh. After the cigar has a chance to cool down, however, the harshness dies away (for now), along with the earthy undertones. The body also dies from a full to solid medium. The first few minutes of cool smoke bring that same black pepper, along with a nice, gentle cream and leather. A bit of a spicy retrohale adds a pleasant pecan tree wood with additional blasts of pepper. Getting through the first third only took about fifteen minutes – a bit of a fast burn – but not too unusual, due to the small ring gauge. This is where the cigar really begins to flourish. A medium-bodied creamy leather has taken over, producing extremely smooth and abundant, rich smoke. The profile consists of pepper, a gentle oak, plain tobacco, and a hint of cocoa and herbal spices. The finish is also very quick – only lasting a few seconds. At this point, the construction is fairing very well. A very loose draw brings enormous smoke output every time, never needing to puff more than once. The first inch of ash was a tiny bit uneven (I suspect due to the cracked wrapper) and also very flowery/flakey – falling in short intervals. Good news meets me as I enter the second half of the Ichiban. For one, the burn has corrected itself perfectly, holding on very tight and with a razor sharp line. Thus the crack was not an issue. Second, during the last half of the cigar, I was never met with any more of the harshness that I experienced from the first light. Some smokers note the cigar maintained a harsh earth and pepper all the way though – but I found this not be the case with mine. This may be due to the cigars getting an extended seven months rest from their release date. Beverage Pairing I also decided to pair my cigar with a Fentimans Cola, a ginger root botanically brewed soda. (Note: I did not pair until the second half of the cigar, so that my tasting would not be affected). When first tasting the Cola, it has a very strong ginger and herbs flavor, along with a general sugar cane and spice. Paired with the Ichiban Tiburon, it really brought out the herbal notes of the cigar, as well as the leather and oaky wood. I was slightly afraid the Fentimans would bring out too much pepper from the stick, resulting in a pepper domination, but I was relieved that it didn’t. At about 45 minutes, I began to reach the end of the Tiburon. I was disappointed to find that a small amount of harshness came back towards the last third, but it wasn’t unmanageable, as it stayed well under a full body. I was pleased to find that the leather and cream lasted throughout the stick, as well as the cocoa popping in and out. Both the draw and burn remained perfect, and when leaving it for a few minutes at a time, it always picked right back up with a burst of smoke from just one puff.
note_sources.title: Room101 Ichiban

note_sources.text: It’s always exciting news when a retired cigar is resurrected, but few have demonstrated this maneuver quite like Matt Booth, especially in the case of Room 101 Ichiban. The first Ichiban came out back in 2015, and was retired, along with the entire brand, not long after. Despite the immense success of the Room 101 brand, Booth was just ready to move on, or so he thought. In recent years, Booth has come out of retirement on the cigar side of things and done several collaborations with such esteemed brands as Caldwell Cigars and La Palina, with his latest offerings being widely accepted by both fans of the old brand and newbies alike. Apparently the sweet taste of success (and Room 101 cigars) got the best of him, leading to the re-introduction of Room 101 Cigars into the current market. Ichiban is among the first cigars to bear the modern Room 101 name, and, unlike its prior incarnation, is sold as an ultra-affordable bundle cigar. Hailing from the sunny Dominican Republic, the new Ichiban boasts a new, modern blend of core tobacco, and, unlike its former release, comes available in 3 delicious variations: Connecticut, Habano, and Maduro. Aside from being unusually easy on the wallet, Room 101 Ichiban virtually offers something for just about any preference. Despite its economical packaging, it is still a premium handmade product using long leaf fillers and top quality tobacco, regardless of the variety. Whether you have enjoyed the amazing Room 101 Cigars of yesteryear or just want to try something new, Room 101 Ichiban fits the bill. Ichiban translates into English as the word “First,” and it’s easy to see how this name is quite appropriate for such a cigar. It is a proverbial no-brainer for any price-conscious cigar fanatic that wants a solid smoke to enjoy on a daily basis.

The first notes are spicy, creamy, and very pleasant. It’s like the Garcias have taken the famous “Pepin spice” and toned it down, making for a muted and subtle take on the well-known profile. Soon the creaminess develops into a more articulate milk chocolate and coffee. There is also a subtle flavor of dark fruit juice in the background and finish of each puff.
note_sources.title: San Cristobal Ovation

note_sources.text: San Cristobal Ovation is one of the newest creations from the all-star team of premium cigar makers Ashton and My Father’s Don Pepin Garcia. Limited to only 3000 boxes of 22 made, San Cristobal Ovation is available in only one size. Made in the My Father cigar factory in Nicaragua, these 6 1/2" by 52 ring toro sized cigars feature a premium blend of Nicaraguan tobacco fillers and binder as well as a double fermented San Andres Oscuro wrappers. This is a great medium-to-full bodied smoking experience.

specs.wrapper: San Andrés Oscuro (2.5 yr double fermented)

note_sources.text: The cap cuts off rather nicely, with minimal tobacco shavings. The draw proves on the loose side, cooling my tongue of tobacco and musty cedar aromas. The San Andrés maduro wrapper takes a good toasting to get lit properly, but once lit, lets off an absorbent amount of smoke output. The initial flavors are a very mild pepper and earth, and the smoke, as voluminous as it may be, feels very light and airy in the mouth—leading to a dissatisfying finish. The draw is definitely on the loose side, and as the burn develops, it seems to be harder and harder to keep the thick wrapper lit. Deep into the first third, some much needed flavor finally opens up, although not as much as I would like. There is a deep and tasty tobacco core, surrounded by pepper, earth, and a little spice on the finish. The retrohale is very easy and adds a nice cream to the palate, both in texture and flavor, which definitely helps the
note_sources.title: Señorial Maduro El Cuadro

note_sources.text: Following the release of his instantly popular Senorial cigars, Jose Blanco has finally brought forth a maduro-wrapped version, first seen at the ICPCR 2015, and since then Senorial Maduro has been gaining huge momentum. Coming out of the Las Cumbres factory in the Dominican Republic, Senorial Maduro is lovingly crafted using top shelf Dominican filler and binder tobacco, exclusively utilizing Piloto Cubano and Criollo '98 varieties. The maduro wrapper of choice for Senorial Maduro is an oily Mexican San Andres maduro, showing Blanco's passion to be head and shoulders above the rest. San Andres maduro wrappers have become the key element for some of the world's finest maduro cigars, and the addition of a San Andres wrapper to the already delicious Senorial blend makes for a cigar that's truly destined for stardom.(See more Senorial Cigars ) Impeccably constructed, Senorial Maduro pours out thick, silky blue smoke. Initially, the full-bodied blast of coffee and cedar pounds hard, but the flavor profile soon settles to a medium-bodied, smooth array of chocolate and earth. Leather notes, as well as hints of cherry and grass, appear along the way, and the finish is always clean and creamy. Senorial Maduro is not hugely complex, but indubitably complex enough to please any discriminating aficionado. The nutty aftertaste seals the deal, making this top notch stick truly a cigar lover's dream come true. For the most part medium-full, Senorial Maduro is a cigar that can really be enjoyed by anyone, but only true connoisseurs will truly appreciate the delicate flavors presented by the masterful blending of Jose Blanco. Senorial Maduro pairs well with scotch or coffee, and is about on the same level of strength and flavor profile as cigars such as Oliva Serie V Melanio Maduro and Padron Maduro . If you loved Jose Blanco's original Senorial blend but have been longing for a maduro version, your dreams have come true. This cigar is not only a wonderful maduro cigar, but a masterpiece that may well become a cigar for the ages.

specs.factory: Tabacalera Palma (Dominican Republic) Production: Regular Release

note_sources.text: Getting the cigar fired up, during the first few puffs the most dominant notes are dark chocolate and pepper—both on the tongue and in the retrohale. As the cigar starts to settle in, hints of barnyard, cinnamon, and hazelnut appear, giving the cigar a very pleasant profile. Just a little farther in, a creamy chai note appears on the finish, adding an
note_sources.title: Southern Draw Manzanita Toro

note_sources.text: The Havana VI Verocú Blue No. 1 fires up quickly, bringing out black peppercorn flavors across the palate, while not being particularly fiery through the retrohale. With a bit more time, nutmeg develops, providing a bit more vigor through the nostrils. The smoke is thin in body and somewhat dry in texture, biting the palate with a lingering black pepper and anise. It’s medium in terms of flavor, strength, and body, with a dry woodsy vibe being the driving characteristic. The cigar creates a flaky ash as it burns, being white with a brown tinge and lasting for about three quarters of an inch. A touchup is needed as the cigar passes the first third, and I can’t help but feel that an under-filled bunch is to blame. Hickory-like smoked woods seem to kick off each puff, with a natural sweetness riding beneath; this is followed by dry roots/stems/licorice through the finish. There’s a vegetal quality to the profile as well, with something along the lines of potato skin bridging the gap of the woody and root-like flavor components. Passing the midpoint, the cigar shows the first signs of a change in profile, with a funky fermented milk note that reminds me of kefir. The smoke is largely bitter on the palate, being picked up on the middle and sides of the tongue most noticeably. The natural sweetness from before seems to leave the cigar after the halfway mark, allowing root-like bitterness to run rampant. The profile shifts to something more along the lines of medium in flavor, medium-full in strength, and medium-plus in body, being largely similar in flavor (darkening as it burns) until its eventual
note_sources.title: Tatuaje Havana VI Verocú Blue No. 1

note_sources.text: Pete Johnson and Jose "Pepin" Garcia have combined in the past to make one of the most renowned cigars on the market, Tatuaje. Numerous different blends and stylings have left the My Father cigar factory in Nicaragua under the Tatuaje name, each a perfectly blended and constructed masterpiece, and Havana VI is no different. Utilizing Nicaraguan filler and binder tobaccos as well as an amazing Nicaraguan Corojo 99 wrapper, this is the type of cigar people rave about when they go on at length about smoking a puro. While some may say Tatuaje Havana VI is medium-to-full body, we found this much closer to the medium range. While lighter than most Garcia blended cigars, fear not. The characteristic spice and flavor profile fans of his cigars have come to know and love is present from foot to nub. (See all Tatuaje cigars ) A simple red band embellished with white fleur-de-lis designs and the Tatuaje name greats the smoker, but that is no accounting for the complexity of flavors that are hidden beneath the wrapper. From first light, the signature Pepin spice will hit you, but not run you over. With each and every puff, Havana VI mellows out and more earthy and woodsy flavors dance on the palate. The spice is there but it seems to almost be an extremely pleasant after thought. The draw is extremely smooth, almost to the point where you don't even have to inhale to let the voluminous smoke enter your mouth. Long white ash formed before we had to tip it off. Tatuaje Havana VI is another fine example of what happens when two innovators in the cigar world get together. Johnson and Garcia have another winner on their hands. The very subtle spice and earthiness to this cigar make it a perfect pairing for smoky scotch or bourbon, or a refreshing IPA.

note_sources.text: Tatuaje Havana VI Verocu is a cigar that has launched the Tatuaje brand to new heights. Originally offered as a limited edition under the Havana VI or "Red Label" line, Verocu has since become adopted as a regular production cigar made by Don Pepin and company down in Nicaragua in collaboration with "Tattoo" Pete Johnson. Verocu is sometimes considered the little brother to Cojonu, another limited edition Tatuaje that became a successful regular production project. Made in masterful Cuban fashion, Verocu consists of an all-Nicaraguan filler and binder blend and a Nicaraguan Habano Rosado Oscuro wrapper leaf. A laundry list of accolades is topped off with a 90-rating from Cigar Aficionado, making the Verocu one of the most respected and recognized cigars to bear the Tatuaje name. (See all Tatuaje cigars ) If there is one thing Tatuaje is known for, it has to be quality. When it comes to Verocu, the quality is second to none. Rolled in classic Pepin style, Verocu is rolled just right, with a fantastic draw and a sharp burn, though slightly crooked due to the fact that Verocu literally oozes with rich oils. Copious clouds of blue smoke gush from the Verocu, slathering the palate with a storm of white and red pepper and earthy nuances. Cocoa, coffee, and a light citrus note complement the peppery backbone while the finish is robust and spicy. Medium-full-bodied and remarkably full-flavored, Verocu is a Nicaraguan masterpiece, reminiscent of the Cubans of old. Verocu is a masterpiece of a cigar. Beginners and intermediates should look elsewhere and leave this one to those with heavily seasoned palates. Classic complexity and spiciness familiar with Don Pepin cigars can and will be found with Verocu. However, it is tame, refined, and relaxing at the same time. Verocu pairs well with your basic scotch, bourbon, and rum, but can best be enjoyed alongside a simple glass of water, as I recommend when it comes to overly complex cigars of this stature. Similar sticks may include the original Tatuaje blend as well as Don Pepin Cuban Classic . For old school Cuban flavor mixed with modern full body and complexity, along with superb construction and an immense quality to value ratio, Tatuaje Havana VI Verocu is an absolute no-brainer.

specs.factory: My Father Cigars S.A. (Nicaragua) Production: Regular Production

note_sources.text: The first light opens with a clean, straightforward profile. Toasted hickory balanced by lightly creamy dark-roast coffee leads the way, supported by a dry earthiness and a restrained black pepper that sits more on the lips than the tongue. The flavor and body are mild/medium at best, and the strength is mild. The finish is clean and moderately long, leaving behind a lingering wood and light spice note. The smoke output is impressive and, even with the snug draw, I am having no trouble getting copious smoke output with each puff. As the cigar settles in, additional layers begin to emerge. The hickory note deepens and takes on a slightly charred edge, while a subtle ground-cinnamon note begins to round out the coffee profile, balancing the pepper and keeping the cigar from feeling sharp or aggressive. Retrohales bring a bit more white pepper into the mix, but it remains controlled and modest. The burn line is wavy, which isn’t surprising from a “Cuban sandwich” roll, though it’s not in need of a touchup at this time. The ash is very firm, holding tight to the cigar. Flavor is medium, body is mild/medium, and strength is mild/medium. Approaching the midpoint, the cigar is feeling like it’s missed its stride. The profile has barely moved—what has changed is not necessarily for the better. The hickory wood is turning into an over-charred and slightly acrid note. It’s reminiscent of the smell that your backyard fire pit gives off the morning after a rainstorm. The creamy coffee note has gotten sharp, giving more of a “latte that woke up and chose violence” vibe. The espresso portion is overdrawn, and the cream is unable to cut it. On a positive note, the burn is slow, and the first ash finally drops into my tray. In the final stretch, the Series P Honduras stays true to itself. The char and coffee notes dominate the profile but aren’t becoming any harsher. Strength creeps up slightly yet remains comfortably below medium. The cream has completely faded, and gone is the ground cinnamon note.
note_sources.title: Tatuaje Series P Honduras Robusto

specs.factory: My Father Cigars Honduras (Honduras) Production: Regular Production

note_sources.text: . Tatuaje Tattoo has an attractive appearance, using a red band with a gold trim. It has a circle band with the Tatuaje Tattoo stamp in black in the background and the word “Tattoo” in white in front of it. Against the dark, coffee colored Ecuadorian Habano wrapper, the band pops and really draws your attention. Tatuaje Tattoo Breakdown Wrapper: Ecuadorian Habano Binder: Undisclosed Filler: Nicaraguan Factory: Tabacalera Cubana S.A. (Garcia family – Nicaragua) Production: Regular release Vitola: 5″ x 50 Caballero (robusto) Price: $5 Pre-light draw is minty sweet, like peppermint candies. The foot smells of sweet cocoa and hay. Toasting produces an aroma like summer night barbecues and distant campfires. First draw has the classic blast of pepper you’d expect from a Tatuaje cigar. There are some sweet notes in the background, but they are so secluded, I can’t distinguish them yet. I’m about an inch in and pepper is still the predominant flavor with that sweetness still lingering in the background. Not a lot of complexity to the Tattoo yet, but it is a nice medium body and it goes great with my coffee. So far the burn is great – it worried me at first, but then seemed to course correct itself and is now a semi-straight line. About halfway through the second third, there is a slight harshness. I find it is because I’m mindlessly plugging away on it, trying to decipher the sweet flavor I am getting. DO NOT rush this cigar! It is a bit temperamental. It takes a few longer breaks in between puffs to cool back down. Flavors are still the same. No changing notes, and the sweetness I spoke of is still in the background. I’m starting to pin it down, but really cannot find a flavor to compare it to. I guess a sugary coffee, but coffee is not a dominant flavor in this cigar. Trust me, I drink a lot of coffee! Coming into the final third and this cigar has some life in it yet! Finally, a new flavor pops up, a meatiness like the taste of steak grilling. Let me try to explain. Pretend you are standing over a hot grill, with a juicy seasoned steak in your hand. Now place the steak on the grill and open your mouth to inhale the aroma as the meat sears. That is the flavor I am getting now. The strength is definitely more medium-full than medium now as well. This cigar’s shining moments are in its last efforts. But it is too little too late and then it’s done. Right at the band, the flavors give out.
note_sources.title: Tatuaje Tattoo

note_sources.text: There seemed to be a big influx of premium and boutique cigar makers putting out five dollar cigars recently, and Tatuaje has jumped on this bandwagon with flying colors. Described by Pete Johnson himself as a "starter tat", this wonderful offering by Tatuaje is a great example of what a cigar in this price range should be. A dark and toothy Ecuadorian Habano wrapper leaf covers a mix of fantastic Nicaraguan filler tobacco. This has all the characteristics that you would expect from a Tatuaje cigar, just a little less refined. (See all Tatuaje cigars ) The band is a beautiful red and black design, but the real star of this cigar is the wrapper leaf. Perfectly dimpled and full of tooth, you know, as soon as the Tatuaje Tattoo is brought to your lips it is going to be a flavor bomb. This cigar is full of that signature spice you would expect from a My Father made cigar. After the initial hit of spice subsides, the pepper remains in the background and a cedar and earth flavor mixes in perfectly. Tatuaje is one of the most beloved boutique cigars on the market, and, with their new Tattoo line, they have a stick for just about everyone. An amazing spiciness and earthiness is mixed perfectly and makes this a great mid afternoon cigar. Perfect with a nice cup of hot coffee or even something a little sweeter like a hot cocoa. After you give this a shot, move up to the Tatuaje Miami like for a real treat.

As good as the Corto may look, you can’t always judge a book by its cover. Luckily for me (and the rest of the world) the Corto smokes even better! Right out of the gate, the cigar bursts forth with flavor, putting my senses at maximum capacity. It took me a few minutes to take in everything this cigar was throwing at me, and that’s not a bad thing. The first few minutes were a powerhouse of flavor and strength, showcasing some pepper, a little spice, a deep, raw tobacco, a strong leather-like flavor, and a little bit of milk chocolate. Yum! It’s important to note as well, the Corto has flawless construction. I’ve smoked a dozen of these, and every single one had the same exact draw and burn as the last—a truly impressive feat. The draw is great, perhaps a little too loose, but controllable. The burn isn’t the best, per se, but I have never had to touch it up more than once, and usually not at all, if I am paying attention to it. Smoking through the first inch of the cigar is my favorite part. The smoke is cool, the flavors are intense, and the cigar is simply beautiful. About an inch down, the bouquet of hearty flavors transitions just a little, giving the sweet side a little edge on the palate. More milk chocolate on the front end of things, with a solid punch of pepper, leather, and cedar trees swaying gently along the finish. Halfway through, the cigar brings about a darker sense of flavors, eliminating a lot of the more sweet flavors. While the milk chocolate and leather notes still remain, they are drowned out by the heavy hitters—deep black pepper, earth, a touch of spice, and a lingering anise through the retro-hale. The construction is always where I expect it to be—great, but not quite perfect. The draw is very enjoyable, albeit a tad loose—while the burn line wavers every now and then. The ash, however, holds on nicely with little flaking. I like to end my Cortos right at the inch mark—any further gets a little harsh. But with an hour-plus smoke time, that’s a minor complaint.
note_sources.title: Warped Corto X50

note_sources.text: A bold cigar from a brand you’ll soon come to love, the Warped Corto is tailor-made for quick and complete smoking satisfaction. Created by brand owner Kyle Gellis as the strongest cigar currently in the Warped lineup, the short stature of these fine medium-full strength vitolas ensures you’ll be able to enjoy a premium smoke from beginning to end during a morning or evening commute, over your lunch break, or even between scheduled meetings throughout the day. Packed with a complex filler blend of robust Criollo ‘98 and Corojo ‘99 tobaccos, each of these Nicaraguan Puros are finished with a flawless shade-grown Jalapa Corojo wrapper of exquisite quality and taste. Expertly rolled and box-pressed, the stubby-barreled Warped Corto cigar is designed to deliver its maximum flavor profile before other stogies have even reached their so-called sweet spot. As soon as the densely-packed foot is set to smoldering, your senses can expect a rush of charred oak and rustic tobacco tastes, with a burst of black pepper spice to be found in the retrohale. Soft leather and creamy caramel are abundant as the stick settles into a razor-sharp burn, with smooth milk chocolate, earthy demerara sugar, and a bit of crushed red pepper as your palate’s boon companions throughout the hour-long smoke. Perfect for fans of succulent Nicaragua frontmarks like the Diesel Esteli or even the chart-topping Oliva Serie V, the Warped Corto is your go-to cigar to fill those moments when a good smoke is in demand, but you don’t have much time. Otherwise, just take them on vacation, to your next neighborhood get-together, or enjoy as many as you wish on a lazy Sunday afternoon. Having a sizable collection of these sticks on hand means you’ll never have to go without.

The Don Reynaldo 10th Anniversary lights up with a dry initial blast, evoking imagery of burning brush. It’s not until the third or fourth puff that a subtle sweetness emerges, gradually rounding out the profile. The retrohale introduces notes of cinnamon and milky caramel, with only a light pinch of spice. A curious flavor of fermented milk lingers through the finish, accompanied by nutmeg through the nostrils. As the experience progresses, the profile livens up incrementally. An almost tart, tangy fermented cream quality develops, creating a chewable, lip-smacking finish. This is complemented by the taste of cut tobacco against the tongue, adding depth and complexity between the retrohale and a lively sensation on the tongue. At about three-quarters of an inch in, the burn line shows a slight wave but remains generally even. The smoke output is medium, while the draw leans slightly to the firm side—a touch tighter than ideal, but not especially concerning.
