Each vitola is expertly constructed and draw-tested to ensure maximum performance and a perfect burn. Upon lighting, a steady stream of dense, aromatic smoke follows an exceptional draw, leaving behind a remarkably tight, gray ash. Rich cedar dominates the opening, soon followed by a classic earthy profile accented by nuances of cayenne, white pepper, and brown sugar . A toasty finish ties the experience together into an undeniably satisfying, Cuban-style flavor bomb . Categorized as medium-to-full-bodied , the CLE Habano is never overpowering, consistently delivering a balanced and refined session. Suitable for all audiences yet intended for seasoned connoisseurs, the CLE Habano is as versatile as it is delicious. Its approachable flavor profile makes it an ideal "everyday" stick for those who enjoy Asylum or Eiroa Classic but desire a more accessible price point. It pairs exceptionally well with bourbon, medium-bodied craft beer, or red wine. Join Christian Eiroa in celebrating his legendary success by experiencing the sheer pleasure of this true Honduran classic.

C.L.E. is one of those names that doesn’t get much time in the spotlight, but everyone still knows they’re some of the best darned cigars money can buy. In recent years, there haven’t been a ton of new additions to the company’s portfolio, but as of late, they have been revamping their core line that put them on the map in the first place. Not only that, but there is a star addition to the core lineup that already has the cigar world going crazy: C.L.E. Maduro . When people see C.L.E. brand owner Christian Eiroa of former Camacho fame and “Maduro” in the same sentence, the first thought that comes to mind is the monster that was the original Camacho Triple Maduro back in the day. Well, relax, folks. This one is a bit tamer and a lot more refined. C.L.E. Maduro has the same Honduran filler and binder blend as its Corojo and Habano counterparts, but the big shift is in the Mexican San Andres wrapper leaf. This change brings about an entirely new take on the flavor profile, one so good that C.L.E. Maduro has already earned multiple 90+ ratings in Cigar Aficionado . A classic, clean-cut cedar cabinet box houses the expertly crafted vitolas. Each gorgeous work of art sports a single black and gold band, one very reminiscent of the classic Room 101 cigars that Eiroa was also a part of. The construction is classic Eiroa style, with an easy draw and a clean burn, and absolutely no shortage in smoke production. A quick blast of black pepper starts things off, and this soon turns into a rich medley of cinnamon, cocoa, and coffee beans. Cedar and red pepper round things out, and a hearty core of intense Honduran tobacco flavor holds the whole thing together. The finish is quick and spicy, and C.L.E. Maduro finishes as a true medium-bodied cigar with a ton of flavor. Aimed at more experienced cigar enthusiasts, C.L.E. Maduro has all the attributes of a classic connoisseur-style maduro cigar. Rich, complex, and velvety smooth, this medium-bodied treat is sure to satisfy even the pickiest maduro fanatics. It pairs well with coffee, dark beer, or port wine, and is similar in stature to such succulent San Andres bangers as La Historia or The Wise Man Maduro . Fans of such dark and flavorful sticks will only be doing themselves a huge favor in trying the cigar in question, as it simply has so much to offer. If you are a fan of rich maduro cigars or you just love Christian Eiroa’s cigars, C.L.E. Maduro is a cigar that certainly deserves a special spot in your humidor.

C.L.E. Prieto is one of the latest cigars from the master of powerhouse cigars himself, Christian Eiroa. Made in Nicaragua, C.L.E. Prieto is not a powerhouse cigar per se, but is the first maduro offering from C.L.E. Cigars, meaning it's bound to be bold, sweet, and darn delicious. Introduced as part of a 2-blend release, Prieto, translating as slang for "dark" is the sister cigar of C.L.E. Chele, which translates as, you guessed it, "light." Prieto is blended with a luxurious recipe of Nicaraguan filler and binder tobaccos and finished with a jet-black USA Connecticut Broadleaf Maduro wrapper. So how did Eiroa do with his first maduro cigar under his own brand name? Pretty good, apparently, as Prieto promptly earned a rock-solid 92-rating in Cigar Aficionado soon after its release, as well as the 17th spot in the famed magazine's Top 25 cigars of 2017. With such tremendous accolades, Prieto has already proven itself as one of the most successful sticks ever released under the C.L.E. brand name. Firmly constructed, oily, and dark, Prieto is rolled with masterful precision to ensure an easy draw and a massive smoke output. Billowing clouds of thick white smoke coat the palate with immense layers of thick, chewy maduro flavor, beginning with earthy tobacco and evolving into a whirlwind of chocolate and coffee. Sweet and nutty throughout, Prieto finishes with a crisp, velvety smooth finish and is never overpowering. Residing just outside the realm of ultra-full-bodied (the range of many of Eiroa's past concoctions), Prieto is heavy on the flavor, yet easy smoking and enjoyable. A true connoisseur's cigar, C.L.E. Prieto was made with the seasoned tobacco lover in mind. A well-developed palate and a taste for fine maduro sticks will definitely help to truly appreciate and enjoy the phenomenal pleasure this stick has to offer. Prieto sits just between medium-full and full-bodied and pairs well with dark drinks such as coffee, port wine, and dark beer. Fans of high-end maduro cigars such as Arturo Fuente Anejo and Liga Privada No. 9 should bask in a sea of satisfaction upon lighting a C.L.E. Prieto. Another similar stick is the modern Camacho Triple Maduro , which still uses the same recipe as the original, blended by the same Christian Eiroa behind this lovely offering. When it comes to bold, luxurious smokes, Christian Eiroa and his team are constantly on the crest of the wave. C.L.E. Prieto is one of his finest examples yet, combining the unique flavors of fine maduro tobacco with the classic high-performance blending skills that only he can showcase so beautifully.

Coming out with a sequel to an all-time great is both a daunting task and a risky gamble, but when Cohiba Black was introduced, the cigar world welcomed with open arms, the maduro-wrapped counterpart to one of the most celebrated cigars of all time. The product of classic cigar wizard Daniel Nunez, Cohiba Black, takes the most desirable characteristics of the original Cohiba blend and adds the rich, chocolaty flavor that old time maduro cigars are known for. Made in the Dominican Republic, this blend features 3-year-aged Dominican Piloto Cubano and Mexican San Andres filler leaves with a Connecticut Broadleaf binder and a jet-black, glistening Connecticut Broadleaf wrapper. When this blend was first introduced, it was a reason for maduro fans everywhere to rejoice, as Cohiba putting their name on a maduro cigar was then unheard of. Packed in luxurious black chests and each vitola bearing a newly redone black and silver band, Cohiba Black screams opulence in its richest form. The roll is just right, allowing for a firm, yet productive draw and a razor-sharp burn from beginning to end. This stick oozes with natural oils, and as the flame hits the foot, a textbook array of classic maduro flavor greets the palate. Espresso, cedar, and dark, earthy tobacco flavor make their presence known, along with accompanying hints of chocolate and white pepper. The finish is impeccably clean and crisp, leaving traces of floral flavors on the nose with each puff. Distinctively medium-bodied and velvety smooth, this is one maduro gem that has earned the right to wear that iconic red dot. While simple classic maduro cigars are usually a go-to for just about any experience level, this blend is in a whole different class. It should be thought of as a connoisseur's maduro cigar, one that combines luxury and ultra-premium quality with the celebrated flavors of old. This cigar pairs beautifully with coffee, red wine, or dark beer, and makes for a great celebration cigar. If you tend to lean towards iconic maduros such as Partagas Black or Arturo Fuente Maduro , Cohiba Black should be right up your alley. Maybe you are a long-time Cohiba fan. Perhaps you just love maduro cigars. Maybe you want something special to up your cigar game. No matter what the case, stepping over to the dark side of luxury with Cohiba Black is a decision you won't regret. SHOP COHIBA CIGARS NOW:

When one of the most well-known cigar brands on the planet introduces a new regular production line, it’s usually a big deal, and such was exactly the case when Cohiba Blue entered the scene. Produced under strict supervision at General Cigar Dominicana down in the Dominican Republic, Cohiba Blue is a more fairly priced alternative to the exquisite high-dollar sticks that usually bear the iconic red dot. The idea of Cohiba cigars releasing an affordable “entry level” cigar ended up being quite the hit, and to this day this delicious concoction remains the easiest way to get into the brand. The recipe consists of a three-country filler blend of Honduran, Nicaraguan, and Dominican Piloto Cubano leaves held together with a Honduran Habano binder. The wrapper is also Honduran Habano, of premium grade and extensively aged, of course. The newly updated packaging looks brilliant, with vibrant blue boxes and textured blue and silver bands that sport a much more modern look than we have become used to seeing from Cohiba. The construction is everything one might expect from this world-famous brand , and the productive draw never fails to coat the palate with rich, flavorful smoke on each puff. Cohiba Blue opens with a distinct creamy texture and rich flavors of white pepper and rolled oats. Soon, notes of cedar and coffee begin to shine through, along with bursts of earthy tobacco flavor. Simple and enjoyable, Cohiba Blue combines just the right amount of flavor and depth to create a tremendously satisfying medium-bodied smoking experience. The words “beginner” and “ Cohiba ” are rarely, if ever, used in the same sentence, but in this case, we might be able to make an exception. If we are being honest, Cohiba Blue is one of those cigars that seems appropriate for just about anyone. Medium-bodied and not overly complex by any means, it is simple enough for a beginner to have some fun with, yet is more than interesting enough to satisfy even the pickiest seasoned connoisseur. It pairs well with bourbon, medium-bodied beer, or coffee and makes a great stick for just about any occasion. Though made in the Dominican Republic, the Honduran flavor really shines on this one, so fans of classic Honduran cigars such as Punch or Camacho will probably feel right at home with Cohiba Blue. A premium quality Cohiba cigar with a delicious blend of tobacco, all at an honest, affordable price point? Believe it or not, such a thing really does exist, and its name is Cohiba Blue.

Cohiba has long been a household name for anyone who has explored the world of premium cigars . For decades, this legendary brand has delivered award-winning Dominican blends, but with the release of Cohiba Nicaragua , the iconic Red Dot line has taken a bold leap into Nicaraguan territory. Produced at the STG Estelí factory in Nicaragua, this blend quickly made waves across the cigar world. Inside, you’ll find a rich filler and binder combination from Nicaragua’s most celebrated growing regions— Jalapa and Estelí . The wrapper is an oily, nearly jet-black Honduran Jamastran Sun Grown Colorado Oscuro , adding another layer of depth. Shortly after launch, Cohiba Nicaragua earned a stellar 91 rating from Cigar Aficionado , cementing its place as a modern favorite. The updated packaging also reflects this elevated experience. The once understated black bands have been replaced with textured silver and gold, still proudly displaying the iconic Cohiba name and familiar Red Dot. The cigars themselves boast a rustic look, evoking the character of Cuban Cohibas , while delivering a profile that stands firmly on its own. Expect a firm but effortless draw that produces thick, creamy clouds accented with black pepper, earth, oak, and molasses . Espresso bitterness and a spicy retrohale round out the complex experience, finishing just shy of full-bodied. Residing on the bolder end of medium-to-full-bodied, Cohiba Nicaragua is a cigar made for seasoned smokers who enjoy rich, layered flavors. Complex yet approachable, it pairs beautifully with coffee, dark beer, or bourbon, making it a perfect choice for special occasions. Fans of bold Nicaraguan blends like Oliva Serie V or Liga Privada T52 will find themselves right at home with this cigar. With Cohiba Nicaragua, one of the most famous names in the cigar industry broadens its legacy, inviting a new generation of connoisseurs to experience the power and elegance of the Red Dot in an entirely new way.

Cohiba Red Dot is perhaps the most iconic cigar in the world . A picture of one should be in each and every dictionary, encyclopedia, and online resource next to the definition of the word 'cigar'. Heck, just replace the definition with the picture and call it a day. Spend the time saved by lighting one up and seeing if you can figure out how to blow smoke rings. With its slow –burning, cool, and fragrant enjoyment, it's not like you'll be rushed. Sit back and take your time enjoying the famously smooth and balanced flavors created by the perfect combination of three types of aged Dominican Piloto Cubano filler, rare and unique Indonesian Jember binder, and sultry Cameroon wrapper. Often called "red dot" Cohibas due to the markings on the band, this exquisite cigar offers a medium-bodied flavor and a strong, smooth and incredibly rich character. Handmade with a toothy Cameroon wrapper and aged mixture of Dominican-grown Piloto Cubano tobaccos, Cohiba's blend sets the standard among today's premium cigars.

Cohiba Riviera covers some serious uncharted territory for the famed Dominican cigar brand. For starters, it is the first box-pressed cigar to ever wear a Cohiba band. In addition, it is the first Cohiba to incorporate a Mexican wrapper leaf. As if that weren't enough, unlike nearly all other Cohibas that come out of the Dominican Republic, this line is made at the STG factory in Esteli, Nicaragua. Long story short, this Cohiba might seem to most like anything BUT a Cohiba. However, this surely isn't a bad thing at all. As for the blend, the fillers come from Honduras and Nicaragua, the binder is Honduran, and the wrapper is a beautiful, oily San Andres leaf from Mexico. This 100% non-Dominican Cohiba obviously seems to be quite unique, and right off the bat it has become quite a revered spectacle in the world of premium cigars. The packaging is refined and modern, including smooth purple boxes and dazzling purple and silver bands. The box press is gorgeous, and the cigars seem to ooze with glistening natural oils. Each vitola is rolled to ensure optimal performance, each and every puff providing a thorough slathering of silky-smooth smoke to the palate. The flavor journey begins with a noticeable, though gentle, burst of white pepper, soon followed by subtle and smooth notes of cedar and chocolate. The core of the profile is earthy tobacco, and hints of coffee and black cherry are detectable throughout. The finish is bold and smooth, and overall Riviera finishes as a well-balanced medium-full-bodied cigar. Any cigar bearing a Cohiba band belongs in the hands of an experienced connoisseur. The top-shelf nature of the brand itself, in combination with such a complex and beautifully blended flavor profile, can only be truly appreciated by those who have been around the block a few times, so to speak. Riviera pairs well with bourbon, scotch, or port wine and makes a wonderful celebration cigar. Anyone that has enjoyed such box-pressed San Andres-wrapped sticks as La Historia or La Aroma de Cuba Mi Amor should certainly look into Riviera. A first for Cohiba in a couple regards it may be, but one thing is for sure: Cohiba Riviera continues the Cohiba tradition of being one heck of a fine cigar. SHOP COHIBA CIGARS NOW:

Cornelius & Anthony Aerial is a beautifully sophisticated blend created with old world Cuban style. Manufactured at the famous La Zona factory in Esteli, the Cornelius & Anthony Aerial is a hearty medium-bodied premium cigar. This Ecuadorian Connecticut is a handsome cigar with refined complexity. Subtle notes of coffee, wood and leather from the Nicaraguan filler tobaccos sing as they marry with its US-grown binder; leaving a lingering sweetness on the palate with its velvety smoke. (Shop other Cornelius & Anthony Cigars)

Now Cornelius & Anthony founder, Steven Bailey, has produced a cigar named for his canine companion (the dog is actually named "Oscar," with "Mr. Sugars" being a nickname). Señor Esugars was in development for three years, as Bailey worked with the craftsmen at La Zona in Estelí, Nicaragua, to get a cigar "rich and decadent with dense sweet flavors and a long creamy finish." The fillers are all Nicaraguan, while the binder is an unspecified USA-grown leaf and the wrapper is Mexican San Andres Maduro. (Shop other Cornelius & Anthony Cigars) The Señor Esugars is quite a firm cigar, showing almost no give save for a few spots scattered among the samples. The wrapper is a dark, earthy brown with a good number of small veins, a fine and dry texture on the fingers, and a generally uniform color that plays well off the scheme of the two bands. Each sample is rolled well, with flat seams and only the most minimal of bumps. The foot is cool and with a thick sweetness, reminiscent of a fresh bag of brown sugar, with complementary notes of berries, bagels, and black pepper. The cold draw is smooth and neither too tight nor too loose, with a bit of damp bark and pepper the most noticeable of flavors, while a bit of simple sweetness glazes the flavors.

As expected, the flavor is on the hearty side in the first puffs of the Crowned Heads Broadway Epicure, with the third cigar notably more pepper-laden than the other two. It also offers a much drier profile than the other two, making me think of a slice of really well-toasted whole-grain bread. Retrohales through the first inch or so are very good, delivering a fairly full and peppery sensation, but not one that is overly sharp in the nose, as it leans towards a blunter sensation. There can also be just the slightest touch of chili pepper heat that adds some complexity and sensation. It’s a very engaging start to the cigar, and one that works for my palate, though I don’t think it would be a morning cigar for me given how lively it is. A little bit of chocolate emerges in the subsequent puffs, though it is subtle enough to think that I could easily miss it if not really paying attention to the nuances of the flavor. After the first inch, both the flavor and retrohale mellow just a bit in their intensity, with the flavor picking up a bit of creaminess and the retrohale just softening the pepper’s impact in my nostrils. Even at its fullest, it’s still a very enjoyable profile, but is at its best when it doesn’t turn everything up all the way, complementing the vibrant start with a slightly mellower section. Flavor is medium-full, body is medium-plus and strength is medium-minus. Construction is very good with no issues, and the cigar produces a solid amount of smoke in this first section. The second third of the Crowned Heads Broadway Epicure starts by further mellowing the flavor, as the creaminess smooths over much of the pepper in the flavor. But in its place, I find a subtle yet very interesting and engaging flavor of a chocolate-covered cherry. It’s also fleeting, as the pepper wants to get back into the spotlight, bringing along a more pronounced earthiness. Retrohales get a bit more peppery as well, though it’s lighter and brighter than it was in the first third. It’s not long before the earth and pepper combination takes the reins and leaves the creaminess to provide a very subtle filling of the cracks, while the other sweetness is long gone. Around the mi
note_sources.title: Crowned Heads Broadway Epicure

note_sources.text: The Crowned Heads J.D. Howard Reserve HR50 has a mottled dark brown wrapper with a bit of shine and toothiness. There’s just a bit of give to the cigar, and the veins are small but noticeable from a visual and tactile sense. The pre-light aroma has a light note of dry tobacco, cotton, milk chocolate, cocoa powder and a touch of pepper, though that mix varies from cigar to cigar, and in one there was a sweetness that stepped forward beyond all those notes. The air moves well in the cold draw, with notes of cedar, a hint of sweetness and a touch of pepper. One cigar in particular had a more pronounced chocolate note, which when combined with the pepper made me think back to a cafe in Playa del Carmen where I would stop and get these fantastic Mexican hot chocolate drinks after a long day. Big notes of beef jerky come off the cigar right when it is lit, but the palate unfortunately doesn’t get any of that wonderful note. A tangy note of wood leads things off on the palate, before the J.D. Howard Reserve delivers a good hit of pepper and spice after a few puffs, along with a more distinct cedar note comes in from the background that starts things off on a medium to medium-plus note. A dry chalk comes into the equation after about three-quarters of an inch and brings along a slight bite to the tongue, while the nose gets a good amount of pepper. Early on, the ash is tight and white in some spots, light gray in others. Throughout the first third I’m impressed with this little wisp of smoke I see coming off the cigar, reminding me that it hasn’t gone out while adding an enjoyable aromatic to the immediate surroundings. Heading into the second third of the J.D. Howard Reserve HR50, there is a strong chalky, peppery note in the smoke that hits the nose hard; it’s not big, bold and peppery, rather almost dry and with a mineral quality. One of the cigars was smoked on a fairly humid night and that touch of moisture seemed to sharpen those notes just a touch more. Past the center line, a bit of damp wood and leather comes out before the flavor and body start to build, drying out a bit and bringing out a slightly sour note that I thought I may have faintly picked up earlier.
note_sources.title: J.D. Howard Reserve HR50 (Prerelease)

note_sources.text: Jericho Hill is the fourth regular production cigar from the fantastic mind of Jon Huber and the rest of the team at Crowned Heads. As with all the other cigars of this fabulous band, Jericho Hill has a name and style inspired by music. A fan of Johnny Cash, Huber wished to make a cigar that had all the integrity and authenticity, as well as the rebellious side, of the "man in black." A setting for the song "Cocaine Blues," Jericho Hill is the town where the sheriff who catches the outlaw Willy Lee is from. All four vitolas' names also coincide either with the song "Cocaine Blues" or other songs off the famous At Folsom Prison album. Made in Don Pepin's My Father Factory in Esteli, Nicaragua, Jericho Hill has the best aged Nicaraguan filler and binder tobaccos and an amazing dark San Andres Maduro wrapper. A stylish and simplistic black and silver band, the flavor is as complex as the music which inspired the name. Jet black, there is a sweetness that wafts past your nose getting you prepared for that first puff. As with most cigars from the My Father factory, the first inch or so is a pepper blast, but that quickly subsides and lets the wonderful flavors of the San Andres Maduro wrapper be the star. Wonderful earthiness and a slight cocoa-like sweetness dances across your palate and finds the perfect partner with the white pepper that exudes through your retrohale. The brains behind the original CAO cigars have another winner on their hands with Jericho Hill. If you like medium-to-full bodied cigars, this is the perfect addition to your humidor. With the accolades this cigar is getting we would be surprised if this didn't get high marks on next year's Best Cigars of 2014. Other great Crowned Heads cigars are Four Kicks and JD Howard.

When the famed Crowned Heads Cigars team was challenged to come up with a value-conscious alternative to their hugely successful Jericho Hill line, they collaborated with a small factory in Nicaragua and Juarez was born. That small factory is called Tabacalera Pichardo, founded by Cuban agriculture expert Eradio Pichardo. Working together, the team of tobacco wizards whipped up a blend affordable enough to be accessible to a wide range of cigar fanatics, yet keeping up with the high standards of the phenomenal boutique blends Crowned Heads has come to be known for. The Juarez blend consists of an Ecuadorian Sumatra binder, Dominican and Nicaraguan fillers, and a rich Mexican San Andres wrapper leaf. The packaging on Juarez, like many of the cigars offered by Crowned Heads, is simple, classic, and almost rustic, yet beautiful and classy at the same time. Simple black and white bands depicting a crowned bull adorn each chocolaty brown vitola. The tobacco is oily and veiny, yet velvety in texture. Juarez is rolled in classic Crowned Heads fashion, allowing for a smooth, extremely productive draw. As for flavors, the smoke starts off woody and spicy, soon evolving into a mixture of chocolate and molasses. Nutty, woody notes appear along the way, along with a long, creamy finish. Medium-full-bodied, Juarez definitely hits the spot every time. Just about any cigar that has ever bared the Crowned Heads trademark has been introduced with experienced connoisseurs in mind. The price tag has usually matched the theme as well. With Juarez, the same quality is available at an unusually affordable price point, making it a cigar that may appeal to a more intermediate audience as well. Juarez pairs well with coffee, dark beer, and port, making it quite a versatile cigar ideal for a number of different occasions. If you have tried sticks such Jericho Hill or Headley Grange and ended up in love, Juarez should be a no-brainer. It isn't every day that a boutique powerhouse like Crowned Heads releases something with the word "value" in mind. Take advantage of this rare occasion and stock up on Juarez to enjoy luxury at a fraction of the price.

What happens when a red-hot brand like Crowned Heads has an ultra-premium cigar made in the world-famous My Father cigar factory? La Imperiosa, that's what! Handmade in what many consider to be the finest factory in Nicaragua, La Imperiosa is yet another world-rocking addition to the glorious Crowned Heads portfolio. La Imperiosa consistas of a full-bodied blend of Nicaraguan filler and binder tobaccos and an extra-oily Ecuadorian habano wrapper leaf—the exact same recipe as Crowned Heads' celebrated 2014 limited release of Las Calaveras, only this stick is here to stay as a regular production line. La Imperiosa is relentlessly strong from the get-go, unleashing a typhoon of Nicaraguan pepper across the palate that remains throughout the experience. Bold flavors of sweet nuts and red pepper bombard the taste buds along with a chewy, coffee-like finish and even more spice on the retrohale. La Imperiosa is definitely not for the faint of heart. Named after an old-time Cuban brand, La Imperiosa is the direct result of cigar fans begging for a re-release of a limited edition cigar. Crowned Heads, always eager to please their clientele, responded with not only a re-release, but a permanent addition to their line of cigars. La Imperiosa is for seasoned palates only and pairs beautifully with coffee or dark beer. It's comparable to My Father and San Cristobal and is built to satisfy even the pickiest of connoisseurs. La Imperiosa is more than a cigar—it's a celebration of the rebirth of a cigar that was supposed to be gone forever.

The Las Calaveras Edición Limitada 2025 LC56 has a bit of a spicy start, at least spicier than I was expecting given what I got from the cigar before being lit. It’s not out of control, and some creaminess helps to counterbalance whatever seems a bit out of balance in the early goings. In the first inch, I also get a little earthiness, adding some depth to the flavor but not as much richness as I might generally prefer. Retrohales are peppery with a bit of a spicy accent, a subtle nuance, but one that’s pretty easy to identify with a bit of attention. There are a few fleeting moments where I get some cocoa powder, and almost more the texture than the flavor, though there is some of that present. By the conclusion of this section, the flavors are well-organized on my palate, though they still feel a bit tight, making it hard to really engage with each one. Flavor starts medium-full but comes back to medium, body is medium and strength is mild. Construction is very good, though there are times I would like to loosen the draw just a touch. The second third starts by holding onto the creaminess, with the more noticeable development being a bit of a pretzel bun on the finish, particularly those well-toasted portions on the top of the bun. There’s also something that seems to go off in its own direction, making me think of black tea leaves at times and the earth gets a touch dustier as well. At the midway point, there’s a notable shift as the pepper gets sharper, while the profile can get a touch chalky, occasionally introducing a mineral aspect, neither of which helps the profile, but both stay limited to accents. The back of this section picks up a bit of toffee and dry nuts, specifically peanuts, but with a bit of cashew and almond as well. The flavor makes one more turn before this section ends: the earthiness deepens and picks up a bit of campfire, while pepper lingers on my tongue after each puff. Flavor is medium-plus in this section, body is creeping up towards medium-plus and strength is still mild. Construction remains very good, with solid smoke production, a pretty even burn line and no combustion issues. As the final third gets underway, I still have trac
note_sources.title: Las Calaveras Edición Limitada 2025 LC56

note_sources.text: Le Carême is a cigar designed from the get-go to be a delectable confection to thrill the palate. Now, we're not saying this is a sweetened or infused smoke because the folks at Crowned Heads are far to wise for that sort of gimmick. Instead, this premium cigar is named after the French chef responsible for popularizing the soufflé, so you can expect a complex concoction full of robust flavor. Rolled at E.P. Carrillo's Tabacalera La Alianza factory, each bold stick is coated with a toothy Connecticut Broadleaf to warmly embrace the Nicaraguan longleaf filler and Ecuadorian Sumatra binder expertly layered within. As a general rule, Connecticut Broadleaf wrappers are rugged in appearance and the one worn by each Le Carême vitola is certainly no exception, although the gold crowns embellishing the elegant blue and white band do put some additional shine to the already oily barrel. From the chocolatey taste to the nutty, earthy aroma, the well-fermented outer tobacco is a perfect vessel to deliver the black walnut, mocha, and stone fruit that infuse the thick smoke soon after lighting. Some pepper and espresso weave in and out during the second third, but it's the ending full of cream, nutmeg, sea salt, and cocoa that's the part worth waiting for. Medium in strength and body while containing the kinds of tastes your palate has been craving, the 92-rated Crowned Heads Le Carême is wonderful with a morning coffee yet can rise to the occasion after a big dinner when paired with an old school cognac or brandy. Make sure to carve out some time to spend with friends and a few of these smokes. It's important.

If the folks at Crowned Heads have a single amazing skill, it is bringing special cigars to the American market, something clearly demonstrated by the introduction of Luciano The Dreamer . When ACE Prime and Crowned Heads laid out a distribution deal a few years back, it was agreed that Nicaraguan factory Tabacalera Pichardo, which is owned by the same people at ACE Prime, would be making cigars for Crowned Heads moving forward. Luciano The Dreamer, named after company founder Luciano Meirelles, is one of the first releases, and to say it was a success would be an understatement. This blend features fillers from Nicaragua and Peru, a Nicaraguan binder, and a smooth Habano Corojo 99 wrapper leaf from Ecuador. Not only did this cigar make a big impression on fans of high-end boutique cigars worldwide, but it also earned a pair of 92 ratings in Cigar Aficionado and a spot on the famed publication’s Top 25 Cigars of 2021 . Simplistic packaging for Luciano The Dreamer includes crisp black and gold boxes and beautifully plain black and white bands on each vitola. The construction is impeccable on this top shelf specimen, yielding an easy draw and massive smoke production. Immediately upon lighting, the backbone of the flavor profile is revealed, a lovely combination of cedar and earth with a sprinkling of white pepper. Bread and chocolate are noticeable along the way, as well as a faint fruity sourness lingering in the background. Spicy pepper is noticeable on the finish, along with a touch of wood. This blend finishes on the very heavy end of medium-full-bodied. All things considered; this is everything but a beginner’s cigar. While never overpowering or imbalanced, the head-spinning complexity of the flavor profile is something only highly seasoned connoisseurs can truly appreciate. It pairs well with bourbon, coffee, or port wine and serves well as a celebration cigar. Tabacalera Pichardo is also the birthplace of Crowned Heads all stars Juarez and Mil Dias, so it is almost a sure bet that fans of either will come to enjoy this masterpiece. Sometimes, you have to treat yourself and enjoy the finer things in life and lighting up an ultra-premium cigar like Luciano The Dreamer is one heck of a place to start!

Luminosa is a cigar from the well-known boutique powerhouse Crowned Heads, made in collaboration with the one and only Ernesto Perez-Carrillo Jr. Produced in the Dominican Republic at Tabacalera La Alianza, Luminosa is a bit different than the majority of cigars bearing the Crowned Heads trademark, as it resides on the milder side of the spectrum. That was the idea, in fact, according to Crowned Heads co-founder Jon Huber. They wanted something more approachable and versatile, rather than the more robust cigars the brand has come to be known for. Luminosa wears a golden Ecuadorian Connecticut wrapper leaf on a Nicaraguan binder and filler. Luminosa is quite the cigar for any connoisseur seeking something light, pleasant, and highly-refined that won't break the bank. Golden brown in color and somewhat rustic in overall appearance, Luminosa is finished with an interesting orange band featuring what appears to be native artwork in the background. As with any other Crowned Heads cigar, Luminosa is beautifully constructed and offers an easy draw with boatloads of smoke. Opening with a slight burst of pepper, the profile quickly settles down into the lighter side of medium-bodied, where it remains for the duration of the smoking experience. Notes of grains, tobacco leaf, and cream are apparent, along with sweet cedar and cayenne on the finish. A light citrus note seems to linger in the background, further adding character to the blend. Simple, enjoyable, and flavorful, Luminosa definitely fits the bill when it comes to versatility. It is the kind of cigar that can be enjoyed at any time of the day. While Crowned Heads is more of a "connoisseurs only" type of brand, Luminosa can certainly be enjoyed by just about anyone. Medium-bodied and packed with flavor, Luminosa pairs well with white wine, coffee, or lighter beer and is a great choice for any occasion. All things considered, Luminosa falls into the same category as versatile premiums such as Montecristo Classic , Romeo y Julieta Reserva Real , and CAO Gold . Whether you are a die-hard Crowned Heads fan or you just want something that can be enjoyed anytime, anywhere, Luminosa makes a great choice.

In a world where so many people are obsessed with instant gratification, it is important to remember that some of the best things in life are worth waiting for. Mil Dias is one of those things: a cigar that took over 3 years to create and one that has taken the Crowned Heads portfolio to an entirely new level. It all started when Crowned Heads co-founder Jon Huber was given a handful of blend samples from the owners of ACE Prime Cigar and Tabacalera Pichardo. The three men in question would spend the next few years tweaking and experimenting, aging, and testing, until finally what is today known as Mil Dias was ready to go. Made in Nicaragua at Tabacalera Pichardo, this blend features a 3-country filler blend consisting of leaves from Costa Rica, Nicaragua, and Peru. The binder is Nicaraguan, and the wrapper is a golden brown Habano leaf grown in the lush volcanic soil of Ecuador. The finished product would end up taking the cigar community by storm, first blowing up on social media and then gathering a pair of solid 91 ratings by Cigar Aficionado. Mil Dias has since become somewhat of a sensation among fans of boutique cigars. Gorgeous wooden chests seat the precision rolled vitolas, each wearing a simple white band bearing the Mil Dias logo. The draw is productive, and the burn is sharp, offering billowing clouds of silky smoke first greeting the palate with smooth woody flavors. Pepper is next up, combining delightfully with the creamy body of the rich, earthy smoke. The sweet tobacco flavors of the unique filler blend form the backbone of the profile, while notes of toast, black pepper, and floral nuances are detectable throughout. There is a final dose of cedar on the finish, wrapping up the delicious creamy flavor journey and rounding things out nicely. After all is said and done, this stick finishes as a medium-full-bodied cigar. This cigar is a great stepping stone between mild and full-bodied smokes and those taking this step will greatly appreciate the complexity and satisfying smoking experience Mil Dias has to offer. It pairs wonderfully with bourbon or scotch and is quite a treat to settle down with when there is plenty of time to sit back and enjoy all the beauty of the flavor profile. Mil Dias is the second Crowned Heads cigar to come out of Tabacalera Pichardo, following Juarez , another stick to blow the minds of small batch cigar freaks worldwide. Mil Dias literally translates “1000 Days,” an appropriate name alluding to the lengthy time period which was required to finish such a fantastic stick as this. The good news is that the wait is over, and now is the time to get your hands on Mil Dias by Crowned Heads and enjoy the small batch cigar that has taken the cigar world by storm.

All three cigars start off with a combination of dark chocolate and caramel sauce sweetness as well as some very light spice on my tongue. Charred meat and cedar quickly take over as the main flavors of the profile. Secondary notes of gritty earth, cocoa nibs, espresso beans, saltine crackers and lemongrass show up at various points, while the retrohale features plenty of black pepper and a dark, fruity sweetness that reminds me of blackberries. Flavor is at full while both the strength and body end the first third at a solid medium. In terms of construction, all three cigars give me no issues whatsoever when it comes to their respective burns, smoke production or draws. The cedar note that was prevalent in the first third recedes to the background during the second third and it is replaced by a stronger powdery cocoa nibs flavor that joins the charred meat note at the top of the profile. Additional flavors include not only the aforementioned cedar but also more gritty earth, citrus peel, bitter espresso, hay and plain oatmeal, while the blackberry sweetness on the retrohale shifts to a caramel sauce sweetness. The flavor remains at full, and while the body stays put at a solid medium, the strength increases slightly to land at a point just over the medium mark. Each of the three cigars has issues with their burn lines, but two of the three eventually correct themselves—the other needs a quick touch-up with my lighter—while the draws and smoke production continue along their excellent paths. Leading up to the final third, there are very few changes in the profiles of the Mil Días Maduro Sublimes, but I am enjoying the flavors so much that I hardly mind. Charred meat and cocoa nibs lead secondary notes of espresso beans, creamy cedar, almonds, hay, sourdough bread and light cinnamon, while the amount of black pepper and caramel sauce sweetness on the retrohale remains about the same compared to the second third. The flavor stays at full, but both the body and strength increase to land at medium-plus and medium-full, respectively. Thankfully, the burn lines are one aspect that do change—for the better—as all three cigars give me no issues in that regard, while the
note_sources.title: Mil Días Maduro Sublime

note_sources.text: Tim Ozgener left the cigar world over a decade ago, vowing that he was, in fact, finished. However, very few cigar icons ever stay away for good, and thankfully for us, neither has Ozgener, as the legend has now returned, partnering with Crowned Heads to bring about his first comeback hit: Ozgener Family Cigars Bosphorus. It was rumored early into his retirement that Ozgener may have been working with Crowned Heads from the get-go, but those rumors promptly fell by the wayside, and the memory of the former front man for CAO cigars faded along with them. For this reason, it came to many as quite a pleasant surprise when his return was announced, and the cigar accompanying it was to be something big. Big doesn’t begin to describe the stellar 93-rated Nicaraguan gem bearing his family’s name, rocking a crazy blend of fillers from the Esteli, Jalapa, and Ometepe regions of Nicaragua. The stick has 2 binders, a Nicaraguan leaf and an Ecuadorian Connecticut. As for the wrapper, they went with a gorgeous Ecuadorian Sumatra leaf, somewhat of a throwback to the standouts of the Cigar Boom era when Ozgener rose to success. This line is named after the Bosphorus Strait, a natural strait in Turkey where Ozgeners parents were born. The packaging for this blend is nothing short of beautiful, featuring colorful boxes and bands with gold accents and big, bold lettering. Ozgener never cut corners on his logos, so this comes as no surprise. The construction is incredible on each and every stick, once again no surprise there, as you might recall that Tim Ozgener is the one that made “draw testing” a thing back in the day. The first thing you might notice about this box-pressed beauty is that the smoke production is almost too good. Billowing clouds of thick smoke fill the room with every puff, and the flavor of the rich blend immediately makes its presence felt. An immediate bombardment of earthy, grassy flavor begins from first light, soon sparked with interesting notes of pine, cinnamon, and red pepper flakes. The earthy core of the flavor profile screams with a heavy presence of aged raw tobacco, and the finish has just a touch of spice. Bosphorus finishes as a full-bodied stick, so it is not for the faint of heart. Back in the day, CAO cigars offered something for everyone, and for the most part, they were pretty acceptable for a wide audience. Such is not the case with Ozgener Family Cigars Bosphorus. This full-bodied, complex beast of a cigar is meant for long-time cigar connoisseurs, likely the ones that enjoyed Ozgeners creations back in the early 2000s. It takes someone with a well-developed palate to truly enjoy such a masterpiece. This cigar pairs well with bourbon, cognac, or full-bodied beer and is best enjoyed after a meal or on a cool evening. Though in pretty much a class of its own, something about it seems similar to cigars such as Allegiance by EP Carrillo or even Padron Natural . If either of those sticks appeal to you, this one will probably put a smile on your face. Maybe you are a fan of Ozgener’s world-famous concoctions from the glory days of classic cigars, or maybe you just want a strong, complex blend that is new and exciting. Either way, Ozgener Family Cigars Bosphorus is a cigar to try.

The first third starts with a very light metallic note, combined with some spice and pepper. Thankfully, the metallic note disappears almost immediately and doesn’t make enough of an impact to affect the profile. Main flavors of powdery cocoa nibs and cedar easily outpace secondary flavors of baker’s spices, peppery earth, sourdough bread, chalk, charred meat and a light cinnamon note, while the retrohale features a combination of light red pepper and caramel sauce sweetness. The first and second cigars feature a slight soapy finish that is a bit off-putting, but thankfully, the third cigar has a more enjoyable espresso note that seems to be getting stronger as the first third burns down. Flavor is full, while both the body and strength hit a point just under medium. When it comes to construction, the draw resistance is excellent, and there is plenty of thick smoke, while the burn lines are extremely straight with no issues. During the second third, all three cigars continue to feature a combination of creamy cedar and cocoa nibs as the main flavors. Secondary notes include toasted bread, cinnamon, minerals, plain oatmeal, dank earth, and dry hay. On the retrohales of the second and third cigars, there is a bit more red pepper than in the first third, but the caramel sauce sweetness remains about the same. However, that is reversed in the first cigar, as the caramel sauce sweetness increases and the red pepper has receded a bit. Thankfully, by the time the burn line reaches the halfway point, the soapiness that was present on the finish of the first and second cigars is long gone, and all three cigars now feature a similar espresso note. Flavor remains full, the body increases to a solid medium, and the strength hits a point just over medium. The burn lines remain a high point, and the smoke production and draw resistance give me no problems. The final third features a bit of a change, as a leather tack note joins the creamy cedar at the top of the profile, followed by additional flavors of plain popcorn, herbs, peanut butter, chalk, gritty earth, barnyard and cinnamon. The retrohales are now more uniform across all three cigars and feature a combination of ligh
note_sources.title: Tennessee Waltz CG

note_sources.text: In 2014, Crowned Heads introduced a pair of cigars that were destined to be regional releases. To be honest, I didn’t really remember much about the cigars other than there was another release— 2015 —and that the series hasn’t been seen since then. For the initial release, there were two 6 x 52 toros made at My Father Cigars S.A. in Nicaragua. The Southern Edition used an Ecuadorian Connecticut wrapper, while the Northern Edition used a Connecticut broadleaf wrapper. Both cigars had a Nicaraguan binder and Nicaraguan fillers. The Mason-Dixon Project Southern Edition is definitely part of the new Connecticut  crowd, a trend that has admittedly died down in the last 24 months, and it works. It’s a Connecticut you expect from the My Father factory and quite honestly, probably the best sans Cabaiguan. While the cellophane shows some signs of age, it’s not yellow, instead just a bit murkier. Once out of the cellophane, the cigar looks a bit weird. It’s not the prettiest shade grown wrapper you’ll see and there’s some noticeable discoloration towards the middle of the cigar. The aroma from the cigar is rather potent, at least for a few seconds, with barnyard, a cantaloupe-like sweetness and some rye bread. Interestingly, after about five seconds, it seems all of the aroma from the wrapper has disappeared. The foot smells both a bit sweet and a bit sour. There’s a generic sweetness and the cantaloupe flavor but they are contrasted by some pine and some sort of sour and acidic mixture I can’t really identify. Speaking of flavors that are hard to pinpoint, welcome to the cold draw. It’s not particularly pleasant and has a bit of a chemical sensation to it. The best I can come up with is something that reminds me of the smell of paste, which leads some fruitiness and a generic barbecue sauce flavor. Put it this way, if this was a cocktail bar, the drink would be sent back. But this isn’t a bar, it’s a cigar review. There was nothing remarkable about the cold draw’s tightness, but the first puff is looser than I was expecting. As such, there’s not a ton of smoke that enters my mouth but I can taste some bread flavors, nuttiness and a creaminess that builds deep into the fi
note_sources.title: The Mason-Dixon Project—Limited Edition 2014 Southern Edition

note_sources.text: For Crux Cigars, the release of the Epicure Habano line in mid-June 2023 was about completing the company’s vision for its Epicure line. “The Habano will complete the Epicure trifecta and we couldn’t be more excited for this cigar to get in the hands of customers across the country,” said Jeff Haugen, president of Crux Cigar, in a press release when the cigar was announced. “We are blessed to work with Plasencia Family making some of the highest quality cigars in the world and the Habano is no exception.” To create Crux Epicure Habano Toro, the company selected a Nicaraguan habano-seed seco wrapper while leaving in place the Nicaraguan binder and filler used for the original Epicure and the Epicure Maduro. For comparison, the red-banded Epicure line uses an Ecuadorian-grown Connecticut wrapper, while the Epicure Maduro uses a Mexican San Andrés maduro wrapper. Here’s what I said about the Crux Epicure Habano Toro when I reviewed it in April 2024 : The Crux Epicure Habano Toro is not just a solid example of a cigar with the word habano in its name, it is a cigar that really leans into the habano profile at several points along its journey from start to finish. The first puffs waste no time introducing the profile, with slight veers away from and back to it throughout, some of which deliver impressive complexity. Construction was also very good, though as I said earlier, I still can’t figure out why it took so long to smoke this cigar. But thankfully, the profile makes those three hours very enjoyable. The Crux Epicure Habano Toro would go on to place #17 on  halfwheel’s Top 25 Cigars of 2024 list. Appearance-wise, the Crux Epicure Habano Toro is a pretty textbook toro, sporting a dark brown wrapper, an average-sized cigar band, and nothing that immediately stands out and catches my attention. For some reason, the word habano— which appears in red ink and a font attempting to look like handwriting and which is tacked onto the word Epicure almost as a red pen correction—catches my eye. It reminds me of when my mom would proofread a paper or some other piece of homework and point out things needing to be fixed, the same way she did for the writers at the newspaper s
note_sources.title: Crux Epicure Habano Toro

note_sources.text: There’s a ton of starch and some umami to kick off the start of the Crux Guild. The former comes in a variety of forms: French fries, peanut oil, raw potatoes. Retiring from the cold draw is the Cointreau flavor, but there’s very little cocoa despite it being all over the pre-light notes. At times, I really struggle to pick out the individual flavors of the Guild, as it’s very compact, but I find a base of creamy cedar and sawdust. There’s lemon, caramel and some mild cilantro underneath it. The finish is almost entirely cedar although I find some black pepper towards the back. Flavor is medium-full, the body is medium-plus and the strength is medium. I make no real mention of construction in my notes, so that’s a good thing. I unfortunately must make notes about the construction in the second third. One cigar has some tunneling issues and the other two both have a need for touch-ups due to unevenness. Flavor-wise, it’s a progression, but not a radical one. Minerals become a much larger part of the profile, eventually turning the Guild grittier. The cocoa returns in the form of a dark but powdery chocolate joined by a somewhat creamy coffee that reminds me of what my Nespresso glass smells like 15 minutes after I finish it and forget to move it off my desk. Minerals continue to increase in their intensity, but there’s a campfire-like toastiness underneath helping to cut through it. In the mouth, there’s almost no sweetness, and the gritty but restrained black pepper isn’t helping. Retrohales of the Crux Guild provide lemon peel and ciabatta bread along with some generic creaminess. At the inch and a half mark, some thyme adds itself into the profile, an odd way to end things, but a decent one nonetheless.
note_sources.title: Crux Guild Robusto Extra

note_sources.text: Starting out, the Crux Limitada Show 2016 features a dominant combination of flavors that include roasted peanuts, earth and creamy oak, along with lesser notes of bitter espresso beans, citrus, and hay. There is a wonderful maple syrup sweetness on the retrohale that has been transported over from the cold draw and it combines nicely with some significant black pepper that is also noticeable. Construction-wise, the draw is excellent after a simple dickman cut, and while the burn is a bit wavy, it is nowhere near bad enough that I need to correct it yet. The smoke production is both dense and copious, while the overall strength starts out quite mild before settling at a point between mild and medium by the time the first third ends. A decrease in the amount of black pepper is one of the significant changes during the second third of the Limitada Show Exclusive 2016, as well as an increase in the maple syrup sweetness on the retrohale. The dominant flavors remain a combination of creamy oak and roasted peanuts with other notes of cinnamon, dark cocoa nibs, espresso beans, leather and anise bringing up the rear. Both the smoke production and draw continue to impress, but the burn has gotten a bit out of hand, forcing me to touch it up twice. The strength has increased noticeably, but not aggressively, and ends the second third still a bit short of the medium mark, although it is still rising. The final third of the Crux Limitada Show Exclusive 2016 shifts a bit again, with the roasted peanut note becoming the singular dominant flavor in the profile, followed by other notes of sawdust, cocoa nibs, creamy oak, leather, earth and a touch of citrus. The maple syrup sweetness that has been so prominent before this point decreases dramatically halfway through the final third, although it is still noticeable enough to impact the profile, and the black pepper on the retrohale is all but gone. The burn has evened up nicely after a rough second third, working together well with both the draw and smoke production, and while the strength level increases as expected, it is still just barely enough to rise a bit above medium by the time I put the nub down.
note_sources.title: Crux Limitada Show Exclusive 2016

note_sources.text: The three Crux Marblehead Maduro Toros I am reviewing have extremely dark brown colors and some of the roughest-looking wrappers I have seen in quite a while: small bumps are everywhere, some of which extend from the body of the cigars so much that they look like knots on a tree. In addition, there are thick, protruding veins all over the place, and the first cigar has a cluster of small dots located at about the middle point that almost look like eggs; more on that in the
note_sources.title: Crux Marblehead Maduro Toro

note_sources.text: We live in an era where, seemingly on a daily basis, another “once upon a time” cigar is being brought back to life. This is definitely the case with Cuba Aliados Original Blend, which is, in essence, the resurrection of one of the biggest brands of the Cigar Boom era. When Oliva purchased the rights to Puros Indios and Cuba Aliados in 2021, the plan was to make 2 separate Cuba Aliados blends. One would be made in the Dominican Republic by E.P. Carrillo for a limited run, and this blend, the Original Blend, would be the regularly produced product, handmade down in Honduras by none other than the Eiroa family, once known for the original Camacho brand. Both plans were executed and both have been hugely successful. This particular blend is made at Julio Eiroa’s Fabrica de Puros Aladino factory in Jamastran using nothing but the choicest Honduran tobacco. That’s right, this cigar is a Honduran puro, and one of just a handful on today’s market, meaning all tobacco—wrapper, filler, and binder—comes from Honduras. A couple of swift 90 ratings in Cigar Aficionado straight out of the gate were proof enough that this stick is a winner, but we will let you be the judge of that. From the classic dress boxes to the revamped brand logo scrolled across each band, it’s evident from the get-go that this is an old school style cigar. Fans of the old Cuba Aliados brand should be taken back in time by the packaging alone. As for construction, well, let’s just say Julio Eiroa doesn’t cut corners when he makes cigars. A soft, productive draw and a boatload of thick, white smoke on each puff ensure that the delicious flavor profile is enjoyed to the full. Speaking of flavor, Cuba Aliados Original Blend starts off with some mild pepper and quickly turns creamy and vegetal, along with some floral bursts on the retrohale. A solid, earthy core holds the entire package together, and the finish is pronounced but clean. Notes of grass, cocoa, and cedar are felt here and there along the way, and after all is said and done, this stick finishes as a solid medium-bodied cigar. Though probably not intended for a younger audience, Cuba Aliados Original Blend is certainly appropriate for cigar smokers of all experience levels. Medium-bodied, fresh, and not exceedingly complex, it serves the purpose as an all-around, anytime smoke for just about any and every occasion. It pairs well with medium-bodied beer, bourbon, or white wine, and is similar in stature to some of the old classics such as Romeo y Julieta Reserva Real or Punch . Whether you want to get nostalgic and compare it to the old blend or want a great new cigar that is enjoyable on every front, Cuba Aliados Original Blend is a rock-solid choice that will never disappoint.
